candidates.subject: Anatomy
candidates.value: The abducens nerve is related to Dorello's canal. The abducens nerve enters the cavernous sinus by passing within this canal. Dorello's canal is an interdural space limited superiorly by the petrosphenoidal ligament, laterally by the petrous apex, and medially by the dorsum sellae. This is a confluence of superior petrosal, inferior petrosal, cavernous sinus and basilar plexus venous sinuses. Dorello's canal anatomy is clinically significant in understanding sixth-nerve palsy and in skull-base surgery, especially for petroclival lesions.

candidates.value: Anterior temporomandibular-joint dislocation occurs due to excessive contraction of the lateral pterygoid, classically with extreme mouth opening such as yawning, laughing, vomiting or dental treatment. Some fibers of the upper head of the lateral pterygoid insert into the capsule of the TMJ and the anterior/medial borders of the articular disc. Contraction can pull the disc forward; excessive opening can cause anterior displacement of the joint. Superior and posterior dislocations are rare and associated with high-energy trauma.

candidates.value: The findings are suggestive of herpes zoster involving the trigeminal nerve. The false statement is that motor innervation is exclusively carried by the maxillary division. Motor fibers are carried by the mandibular division. The trigeminal nerve (CN V) is the largest cranial nerve and has ophthalmic (V1), maxillary (V2) and mandibular (V3) divisions. V1 supplies sensation to the scalp, cornea, conjunctiva, iris, upper eyelid, lacrimal gland, forehead and mucous membranes of the nose. V2 supplies lower eyelid, cheeks, maxillary sinus, nasal cavity, lateral nose, upper lip, palate, teeth and gingiva. V3 supplies sensation to the chin/lower lip, temporal membrane, mylohyoid, anterior belly of digastric and mandibular teeth, and provides motor supply to the muscles of mastication, tensor veli palatini and tensor tympani.

candidates.value: The presentation is Frey's syndrome, involving the auriculotemporal nerve, marked 2. The other numbered structures are maxillary nerve, posterior auricular nerve and inferior alveolar nerve. The auriculotemporal nerve is a branch of the posterior division of mandibular nerve and provides cutaneous sensation to the tragus and adjoining external acoustic meatus and to the auricle/scalp. It carries postganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers from the otic ganglion to the parotid. After parotid surgery, aberrant regeneration of these fibers to sweat glands and skin vessels causes gustatory sweating, warmth and redness during salivation.

Clinical points include sensory loss after injury, Frey's syndrome relationship, and use in nerve grafting.

Structures present in the parotid gland from superficial to deep are the facial nerve, retromandibular vein, and external carotid artery. The parotid gland is derived from ectoderm.

candidates.subject: Anatomy
candidates.chapter: Glands of the Head and Neck
candidates.value: The facial artery is not present within the parotid gland. The gland contains the external carotid artery, which terminates as maxillary and superficial temporal arteries, and the transverse facial artery, a branch of the superficial temporal artery. Sometimes the external carotid artery gives the posterior auricular artery within the gland. Veins include maxillary and superficial temporal veins, which unite to form the retromandibular vein. Nerves include the facial nerve and its branches; parotid lymph nodes are also present.

candidates.subject: Anatomy
candidates.chapter: Glands of the Head and Neck
candidates.value: The secretomotor fibres from the glossopharyngeal nerve relay through the otic ganglion before supplying the parotid gland. The otic ganglion is medial to the mandibular nerve. Relations: superiorly - foramen ovale; laterally - mandibular nerve; medially - tensor veli palatini; posteriorly - middle meningeal artery. The otic ganglion is a parasympathetic ganglion below the foramen ovale. Preganglionic fibres originate in the inferior salivatory nucleus and pass through the lesser petrosal nerve, the continuation of the tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve, and relay in the ganglion. Postganglionic fibres pass via communicating branches to the auriculotemporal nerve and supply the parotid gland.

candidates.subject: Anatomy
candidates.chapter: Glands of the Head and Neck
candidates.value: The case is suggestive of parasympathetic stimulation of the salivary glands, causing increased salivary secretion. Parasympathetic fibres to the parotid gland are carried by the lesser petrosal nerve. Preganglionic fibres originate in the inferior salivatory nucleus, travel via the glossopharyngeal nerve and tympanic plexus into the lesser petrosal nerve, and relay in the otic ganglion. Postganglionic fibres travel through communicating branches to the auriculotemporal nerve and supply the parotid gland. The greater petrosal nerve carries secretomotor fibres to the pterygopalatine ganglion and supplies lacrimal, nasal, and palatine glands. Sympathetic supply to the parotid comes from the plexus around the middle meningeal artery. Sensory supply to the gland is via the auriculotemporal nerve, and to the capsule via the greater auricular nerve.

candidates.subject: Anatomy
candidates.chapter: Glands of the Head and Neck
candidates.value: The parotid duct or Stensen's duct opens opposite the 2nd upper molar tooth. It pierces the buccinator at the level of the 3rd upper molar tooth. Structures pierced by the parotid duct are buccal pad of fat, buccopharyngeal fascia, buccinator muscle, and mucous membrane. Clinically, sialolithiasis is more common in the submandibular gland than the parotid. Parotid duct stones are usually radiolucent and rarely visible on plain radiography; contrast is given during sialography to visualize stones.

candidates.subject: Anatomy
candidates.chapter: Glands of the Head and Neck
candidates.value: The accessory parotid gland is present between the parotid duct and zygomatic arch. It is usually a detached part of the parotid gland, with its own blood supply and a secondary duct draining into the main parotid duct. It can be missed during complete parotidectomy, can present as mid-cheek masses, and its histological characteristics can differ from the main gland, so tumors may show a different clinical course.

candidates.subject: Anatomy
candidates.chapter: Glands of the Head and Neck
candidates.value: Frey's syndrome occurs due to aberrant innervation of the auriculotemporal nerve and is also known as gustatory sweating or auriculotemporal syndrome. It commonly develops after parotid surgery or trauma with injury to the parotid capsule. During regrowth, an aberrant connection develops between parasympathetic fibres supplying the parotid gland (auriculotemporal nerve) and sweat glands. This causes sweating, warmth, and redness of the face during salivary stimulation by smell or taste of food. Management includes antiperspirants (aluminum chloride), tympanic neurectomy, and botulinum toxin injection into affected skin.

candidates.subject: Anatomy
candidates.chapter: Glands of the Head and Neck
candidates.value: The newly discovered salivary glands are predominantly present over the torus tubarius, the anatomical structure formed by cartilage supporting the entrance of the auditory tube. The proposed name is tubarial salivary glands. They extend caudally to the pharyngeal wall and cranially to Rosenmuller's fossa. PSMA PET/CT can visualize these glands with high sensitivity and specificity. Radiotherapy over their location has been reported to cause xerostomia and dysphagia; sparing them might improve quality of life.

candidates.value:
The anterior two-thirds of the tongue is demarcated from the posterior one-third by the terminal sulcus, also known as the sulcus terminalis.

Sulcus terminalis divides the tongue into anterior and posterior parts. The anterior or oral part faces superiorly and the posterior or pharyngeal part faces posteriorly.

Sigmoid sulcus is present on the mastoid surface of the temporal bone. Gingival sulcus is present between a tooth and the surrounding gingival tissue. Median sulcus is the central sulcus present on the tongue.

The structure marked A shows the foliate papillae, which lie bilaterally on either side of the tongue near the sulcus terminalis.

Filiform papillae are minute cylindrical or conical projections mainly on the dorsal anterior two-thirds. Fungiform papillae are large, rounded, red papillae mainly on the lingual margins and dorsal surface. Foliate papillae are red, leaf-like mucosal ridges present bilaterally near the sulcus terminalis. Circumvallate papillae are large cylindrical structures, around 8-12 in number, arranged in a V-shaped row immediately anterior to the sulcus terminalis.

candidates.subject: Anatomy
candidates.value:
The image shows deviation of the tongue to the left; the left genioglossus is paralyzed.

When both genioglossi contract they protrude the anterior tongue in the midline. When one contracts, it protrudes and pushes the tongue to the opposite side. Genioglossus also depresses the central tongue and is supplied by the hypoglossal nerve.

With hypoglossal nerve palsy, the ipsilateral genioglossus is paralyzed and the protruded tongue deviates toward the affected side because of unopposed contraction on the normal side.

Genioglossus is attached to the genial tubercle and helps prevent the tongue from falling backward and obstructing respiration; the source notes this as the safety muscle of the tongue.

The image shows a cleft palate. Sensory supply to the palate is not provided by the hypoglossal nerve, which is a pure motor nerve.

General sensation from most of the soft palate is carried by the lesser palatine nerve (V2), pharyngeal branches of the glossopharyngeal nerve, and the plexus around the tonsil. Taste from the oral surface of the soft palate is carried by the lesser palatine nerve; taste fibres initially travel in the greater petrosal nerve, a branch of the facial nerve, and traverse the pterygopalatine ganglion without synapsing.

All muscles of the soft palate are supplied through the pharyngeal plexus (CN X) except tensor veli palatini, which is supplied by the mandibular nerve. The hard palate is supplied by the greater palatine and nasopalatine branches of the pterygopalatine ganglion.

It lies between the superior edge of subscapularis and the anterior edge of supraspinatus, with the coracoid as the medial boundary of the interval. It is reinforced by the coracohumeral ligament, superior glenohumeral ligament, and fibres from the supraspinatus tendon laterally.

candidates.value: The average carrying angle is approximately 17 degrees. It is the angle between the fully supinated forearm and the long axis of the humerus when the elbow is fully extended. It is usually about 10-15 degrees in males and more than 15 degrees in females, varies among individuals, and increases with age. Clinically, the contralateral side should be compared. The source notes that about 5-15 degrees is considered normal clinically; the carrying angle decreases in cubitus varus and increases in cubitus valgus.

candidates.subject: Anatomy
candidates.value: The middle radioulnar joint is a fibrous joint (syndesmosis). Radius and ulna are united by the proximal radioulnar joint, middle radioulnar joint, and distal radioulnar joint. The middle radioulnar joint is formed by the oblique cord and interosseous membrane as syndesmoses. candidates.value: Tenderness in the shown hypothenar region with pain radiating to the ring and little finger is suggestive of a hook of hamate fracture. The pain distribution is related to the close proximity of the ulnar nerve, particularly its deep branch. The hamate is a cuneiform carpal bone with a hamulus (hook) projecting from the distal part of its rough palmar surface. candidates.subject: Anatomy
candidates.chapter: Fossae and Spaces of the Upper Limb
candidates.value: The fascia around the axillary vessels and brachial plexus is called the axillary sheath. It is derived from the prevertebral fascia. Clinical correlations in the source: in a brachial plexus nerve block the axillary sheath localizes anaesthetic solution to the plexus; a chronic retropharyngeal abscess in tuberculosis may spread to the axilla or superior mediastinum, but it never spreads to the posterior mediastinum because the supravertebral fascia fuses there to restrict spread.

candidates.chapter: Fossae and Spaces of the Upper Limb
candidates.value: The image shows an infection of the pulp space of a finger, or whitlow. It requires incision and drainage because, if neglected, it can lead to necrosis of the distal 4/5th of the terminal phalanx. It does not cause necrosis of the entire phalanx because the proximal 1/5th is spared where the artery does not cross the fibrous septa. The pulp space contains subcutaneous fat arranged in tight compartments formed by fibrous septa from skin to periosteum. Complications include ischemic necrosis of the distal 4/5th of the terminal phalanx, osteomyelitis, flexor tenosynovitis and septic arthritis of the distal interphalangeal joint.

candidates.subject: Anatomy
candidates.value: Alveolar epithelium is cuboidal in the resting phase and columnar during lactation, so the statement that it is columnar in the resting phase is false. Fibrous stroma forms septa (suspensory ligaments of Cooper) anchoring skin and gland to pectoral fascia; it forms the major part of the gland but is absent beneath the areola and nipple. During development, thoracic ectodermal ingrowths form 15-20 solid buds that canalize into lactiferous ducts and secretory alveoli. Contraction of myoepitheliocytes facilitates passage of milk along the ducts. The 15-20 lactiferous ducts converge toward the nipple and form lactiferous sinuses.

candidates.subject: Anatomy
candidates.value: Mammary gland cells secrete milk protein (casein) by merocrine secretion, while milk lipid is secreted by apocrine secretion. Therefore breast-milk secretion combines apocrine and merocrine mechanisms. The source summarizes gland secretion types: merocrine - vesicles fuse with plasma membrane and release their contents; apocrine - the apical portion of the cell is pinched off for secretion (examples include milk fat, atypical sweat glands and ceruminous glands); holocrine - the entire gland cell disintegrates to liberate secretion (e.g., sebaceous glands). Eccrine sweat glands were formerly classified as eccrine but are now placed under merocrine.

candidates.subject: Anatomy
candidates.value: Lymphatics from the upper outer quadrant of the breast drain first into the anterior axillary lymph nodes, which therefore function as sentinel nodes in this setting. A sentinel node is the first lymph node receiving lymphatic drainage from a tumor and may be removed during surgery for histopathological assessment of metastasis. Axillary nodes receive more than 75% of breast lymph. The source also classifies axillary nodes relative to pectoralis minor: Level 1 (low nodes) below pectoralis minor; Level 2 (middle nodes) behind the muscle; Level 3 (apical/upper nodes) between the upper border of pectoralis minor and lower border of clavicle. Nodes between pectoralis major and minor are interpectoral (Rotter's) nodes.

candidates.subject: Anatomy
candidates.value: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Horner's or Bernard-Horner's syndrome. It can be caused by a lesion of the white ramus of T1. Horner's syndrome is characterized by a constricted pupil (miosis), drooping of the upper eyelid (ptosis), and absence of sweating of the face (anhidrosis), due to disruption of sympathetic nerve supply. In the autonomic nervous system, the sympathetic outflow is thoracolumbar and parasympathetic outflow is craniosacral. The sympathetic chain receives white ramus inflow (preganglionic fibers) and gives gray ramus outflow (postganglionic fibers); white rami occur from T1-L2. In this setting sympathetic inflow at T1 is disrupted.

The radial nerve (C5-T1) is the largest branch of the plexus and arises as a terminal branch of the posterior cord. Variations include a C4 pre-fixed plexus and T2 post-fixed plexus.

Other branches arising from the cords are infraclavicular.

candidates.subject: Anatomy
candidates.value: Upper trunk injury causes Erb or Erb-Duchenne palsy. It produces adduction and medial rotation at the shoulder, not abduction. The usual mechanism is excessive separation of head and neck, including birth injury, damaging C5-C6. Affected nerves include suprascapular, axillary, musculocutaneous, and radial nerves. The classic waiter's-tip posture includes arm adducted and medially rotated, elbow extended, forearm pronated, and sensory loss along the outer aspect of the arm.

candidates.subject: Anatomy
candidates.value: The axillary nerve, also called the surgeon's nerve, may be injured during inadvertent intramuscular injection. It is a branch of the posterior cord, exits the axilla through the quadrangular space, winds around the surgical neck of the humerus, and gives upper lateral cutaneous nerve of arm supply over the lower deltoid. Injury can follow surgical-neck fracture, inferior shoulder dislocation, or IM injection and may cause regimental-badge anesthesia. Named nerves listed by the source: labourer's nerve = median nerve; musician's nerve = ulnar nerve; surgeon's nerve = axillary nerve; nerve of Bell = long thoracic nerve.

candidates.value: The median nerve is not directly related to the humerus. The axillary nerve is related to the surgical neck, the ulnar nerve to the medial epicondyle, and the radial nerve to the spiral/radial groove. The median nerve arises from lateral and medial cords, gives no muscular branch in the axilla and arm, supplies most superficial flexors in the forearm, passes between the two heads of pronator teres and gives the anterior interosseous nerve, gives a palmar cutaneous branch before the flexor retinaculum, and divides distally into recurrent and palmar digital branches.

candidates.subject: Anatomy
candidates.value: Median nerve injury at the wrist is tested by contraction of abductor pollicis brevis; loss of thumb mobility/opposition can be tested by the pen test. Flexor pollicis brevis paralysis may occur with median nerve injury at the arm/elbow. Benediction-hand and Ochsner clasping tests are used for more proximal median lesions. The lateral half of the palm is supplied by the palmar cutaneous branch and is usually spared in carpal tunnel/wrist lesions because the branch does not pass through the carpal tunnel. Ring-finger sensation is not an isolated median-nerve test.

candidates.subject: Anatomy
candidates.value: The marked sensory territory is supplied by the median nerve. Ape-thumb deformity is seen with median nerve lesions irrespective of site because it reflects distal denervation and non-use atrophy of the thenar muscles except adductor pollicis. The median nerve supplies the superficial flexor group except flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus; its anterior interosseous branch supplies flexor pollicis longus, pronator quadratus, and lateral half of FDP; recurrent branch supplies thenar muscles except adductor pollicis; palmar digital branches supply the lateral two lumbricals and skin of the lateral 3½ digits. Adductor pollicis and medial half of FDP are ulnar supplied, while wrist drop is a radial-nerve palsy.

candidates.value: The base of the heart is formed mainly by the left atrium, so left atrial enlargement can compress the left recurrent laryngeal nerve and cause hoarseness. candidates.subject: Anatomy
candidates.value: The aorta lies anterior to the transverse pericardial sinus. The source explains that serous pericardial reflections form one tube around the aorta and pulmonary trunk and another around the venae cavae and pulmonary veins. The oblique sinus is a J-shaped recess posterior to the left atrium, while the transverse sinus is the passage between these arterial and venous reflections. The aorta and pulmonary trunk lie anterior to the transverse sinus, with the superior vena cava and atria posterior. This permits clamping of the great arterial outflow vessels during cardiac surgery.

candidates.value:
Latissimus dorsi is not an accessory muscle of inspiration. It is an accessory muscle of expiration.

Accessory muscles of inspiration: sternocleidomastoid; scalene muscles; serratus posterior and anterior; erector spinae; pectoralis major and minor.

Breathing involves changing the thoracic volume by altering the vertical, transverse, and anteroposterior dimensions of the thorax. The diaphragm is the key muscle in respiration.

This nerve supplies the cardia and fundus of the stomach. It is called a criminal nerve because it is often missed during a vagotomy procedure and can result in recurrent peptic ulcer disease.

The sympathetic supply arises from T5-T12 spinal segments and reaches the stomach through the greater and lesser splanchnic nerves and the coeliac plexus. It causes vasoconstriction, constriction of the pyloric sphincter with inhibition of gastric motility, and carries visceral pain sensations.

The parasympathetic supply arises from the right and left vagus nerves. The anterior vagal trunk is formed from the left vagus nerve, whereas the posterior vagal trunk is formed from the right vagus nerve. Parasympathetic actions include secretomotor supply to gastric glands, motor supply to gastric musculature, relaxation of the pyloric sphincter with promotion of gastric emptying, and carriage of sensations such as fullness, nausea, and probably pain.

The middle and left colic arteries contribute to the formation of the marginal artery of Drummond at the splenic flexure. The splenic flexure (Griffith's point) is a watershed area of the colon that is more prone to ischemia.

candidates.subject: Anatomy
candidates.value:
The external anal sphincter is made up of striated muscle fibres. It is not a continuation of the outer longitudinal muscle of the rectum.

The external anal sphincter has upper (deep) and lower (subcutaneous or superficial) parts. The pudendal nerve innervates it and it is under voluntary control.

The internal anal sphincter is the terminal thickened part of the inner circular muscle of the large intestine. It extends from the anorectal junction to the anal verge. It is autonomically innervated: parasympathetic activity causes relaxation and sympathetic activity causes contraction.

The conjoint longitudinal muscle lies between the internal and external anal sphincters. It is the continuation of the outer longitudinal muscle of the rectum. Its fibres distally fan out and traverse the internal and external anal sphincters. It has a protective effect on haemorrhoids and degenerates with age.

Treitz's muscle is the submucosal muscle of the anal canal. It is attached to the conjoint longitudinal muscle by Park's ligament, maintains the integrity of the anal cushions, and plays an important role in preventing haemorrhoids.

candidates.value:
Three transverse mucosal folds, also known as Houston's valves, are commonly present in the rectum.

The transverse mucosal folds are permanent and become very prominent on distension of the rectum. The superior transverse fold is present near the beginning of the rectum and may occasionally encircle the entire lumen. The middle transverse fold is the largest and constant fold, present above the rectal ampulla, and projects from the anterior and right wall of the rectum. The inferior transverse fold is the most variable and is found on the left side.

Apart from these, the rectal mucosa has several longitudinal folds that disappear on distension of the rectum.

Ito cells, or hepatic stellate cells, are marked as 3 in the histological image and store vitamin A. They are present in the space of Disse and are mesenchymal in origin.

They have two states. In the dormant state, they store the fat-soluble vitamin A in lipid droplets and are a significant source of growth factors involved in liver homeostasis and regeneration. In the active state, after liver injury they replace damaged hepatocytes with collagenous scar tissue leading to hepatic fibrosis and secrete intralobular matrix components including collagen type III (reticular) fibres.

The space of Disse lies between a hepatocyte and a sinusoid. It contains interstitial fluid, microvilli of adjacent hepatocytes and fine collagen fibres (mostly type III). Lymph produced in the liver drains through the perisinusoidal space of Disse and periportal clefts of Mall into larger lymphatics.

The phrenicocolic ligament connects the splenic flexure of the colon to the diaphragm. It is not attached to the spleen, but lies below it and supports its lower pole. When the spleen gets enlarged, the phrenicocolic ligament along with the splenic flexure restricts its downward displacement.

The phrenicocolic ligament functions as a potential barrier to spread of infection between the left paracolic gutter and the left subphrenic space.

candidates.value:
The right renal vein forms a posterior relation of the head of the pancreas, so it may be invaded by posterior expansion of a carcinoma of the head of the pancreas.

Posterior relations of the head include right renal vein, right renal artery, inferior vena cava, common bile duct embedded in the head, right crus of the diaphragm, and termination of the right gonadal vein. Anterior relations include the first part of the duodenum and origin of the transverse mesocolon.

Relations of the neck: anteriorly the lesser sac, pylorus, and anterior superior pancreaticoduodenal branch of the gastroduodenal artery; posteriorly the portal vein, superior mesenteric vein, and inferior mesenteric vein in about one-third of individuals.

Clinical note: Cancers arising from the head or neck of the pancreas are difficult to operate on because of the confluence of so many vessels near them; this also makes blood-borne spread faster.

candidates.value:
The structure marked A in the image is the Ampulla of Vater.

The bile duct and pancreatic duct unite to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla (ampulla of Vater) within the second part of the duodenum, which opens at the major duodenal papilla.

Sometimes an accessory pancreatic duct is present and opens into the minor duodenal papilla, about 2 cm proximal to the major duodenal papilla in the second part of the duodenum.

Clinical note: Familial adenomatous polyposis (APC gene defect) is associated with carcinoma of the Ampulla of Vater. Duodenal villous adenomas are commonly found around the ampulla and may be premalignant. Duodenal injuries with tissue loss distal to the major duodenal papilla and proximal to the superior mesenteric vessels are best treated in the source note by Roux-en-Y duodenojejunostomy.

candidates.subject: Anatomy
candidates.value:
The entire posterior surface of the pancreas is devoid of peritoneum.

The posterior surface lies over the fascia of Toldt in front of the aorta. The splenic vein traverses directly on this surface.

Only parts of the uncinate process where the superior mesenteric vessels descend on it are also devoid of peritoneum. The entire anterior surface of the body is covered by peritoneum and the tail lies between layers of the splenorenal ligament, which is formed from peritoneum.

Note that the pancreas is a retroperitoneal organ except for the tail; in that sense it is not enveloped by peritoneum, but the anterior surface is in contact with peritoneum.

candidates.subject: Anatomy
candidates.value:
Pancreas divisum has been depicted in the image marked 3.

The pancreas has two ducts that normally fuse during embryological development. The accessory (dorsal) pancreatic duct of Santorini drains the upper part of the anterior portion of the pancreatic head. The main pancreatic duct of Wirsung usually runs within the substance of the gland from left to right.

When the ventral and dorsal ducts fail to fuse, pancreas divisum results. In this condition, most of the pancreas drains through a dominant dorsal duct that enters the duodenum at the minor papilla. A short ventral duct, along with the bile duct, drains to the major duodenal papilla. Therefore, major pancreatic drainage is via the dorsal duct, which opens at the minor papilla.

Patients are usually asymptomatic; however, 25-28% of these patients may experience recurrent pancreatitis that may progress to chronic pancreatitis.

Image A shows normal pancreatic ducts with communication between main and accessory ducts. Image B shows normal pancreatic ducts with no communication between main and accessory ducts. Image D shows absence of the accessory pancreatic duct.

Seminal vesicles do not store sperms. Seminal vesicles are paired accessory glandular structures of the male reproductive system located at the base of the prostate. The duct of the seminal vesicle joins with vas deferens to form the ejaculatory duct. The mucosa of the seminal vesicle is highly folded and is lined by pseudostratified columnar epithelium. They secrete white-yellow viscous fluid and contribute to at least two-thirds of the volume of the semen. Secretions are rich in fructose, coagulation proteins, and prostaglandins. They are alkaline

and play an important role in the motility and metabolism of the sperms. The vesiculo-deferential artery, a branch of the umbilical artery is the primary arterial supply of the seminal vesicles. Additional blood supply is from the inferior vesical artery. Venous drainage is by the vesiculo-deferential veins and inferior vesical plexus. Lymphatic drainage is to the internal iliac nodes

The lining epithelium of the fallopian tube is a single layer of ciliated columnar epithelium. It is similar to the epithelium of the bronchioles.

The ciliated epithelial cells are predominant in the distal part of the fallopian tube. There is an increase in the height and number of cilia during the estrogenic phase of the menstrual cycle.

Other cells include secretory or peg cells, maximally located in the proximal portion of the tube; these are active around ovulation and their secretions help in capacitation of sperms. Intraepithelial lymphocytes may occasionally be present.

Option A: stomach epithelium is simple columnar. Option B: tracheal epithelium is pseudostratified ciliated columnar. Option D: proximal convoluted tubule epithelium is cuboidal with microvilli.

The structure marked is the lacunar ligament.

Lacunar (Gimbernat's) ligament is a thick triangular band of tissue formed from fibres of the medial end of the inguinal ligament and fascia lata. It forms the medial wall of the femoral canal, and the apex of the triangle is attached to the pubic tubercle.

The inguinal (Poupart's) ligament is the thickened external oblique aponeurosis stretched between the ASIS and pubic tubercle. The pectineal (Astley-Cooper's) ligament is a strong fibrous band extending laterally along the pectineal line from the pectineal attachment of the lacunar ligament. The conjoint tendon is formed by the common aponeurosis of internal oblique and transversus abdominis and inserts into the pubic crest/pectineal line.

The fibres of the iliopubic tract fan out with fascia iliaca laterally.

The iliopubic tract is a thickening of the transversalis fascia lying immediately posterior to the inguinal (Poupart's) ligament. It extends from the ASIS superolaterally and arches across the front of the femoral sheath.

Medially, its fibres insert broadly into the pubic tubercle and pectineal line behind the conjoint tendon. Laterally, its fibres fan out within the transversalis fascia and fascia iliaca without bony attachment to the iliac spines.

Clinical note: it is an important landmark in laparoscopic hernia surgery.

The structure involved in causing lurching gait in the child is gluteus medius, marked as 2.

Gluteus medius originates from the outer surface of the ilium between the anterior and posterior gluteal lines and inserts on the lateral surface of the greater trochanter. It is supplied by the superior gluteal nerve.

Gluteus medius and minimus are powerful abductors of the hip joint. When the leg on one side is lifted, the gluteus medius and minimus on the opposite supported side exert traction on the hip bone and raise the pelvis slightly on the unsupported side, helping maintain the trunk upright.

These actions are affected by superior gluteal nerve injury, fracture of the neck of femur, or loss of normal shaft angulation. With paralysis, the pelvis sinks on the unsupported normal side when standing on the affected limb, producing a positive Trendelenburg sign and a characteristic lurch toward the affected side with contralateral pelvic drop.

It supplies the skin on the medial side of the knee, leg and foot as far as the first metatarsophalangeal joint.

The gait shown is characteristic of a left superior gluteal nerve injury causing a positive Trendelenburg sign.

Gluteus medius and minimus are supplied by the superior gluteal nerve. When the opposite leg is lifted, these abductors on the supported side raise the pelvis on the unsupported side and keep the trunk upright.

Inferior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus maximus.

Foot drop is caused by damage to the common peroneal nerve.

The common peroneal nerve is a component of the sciatic nerve. It curves around the neck of the fibula deep to peroneus longus and divides into superficial and deep peroneal nerves.

The superficial peroneal nerve supplies peroneus longus and brevis and most of the dorsum of the foot. The deep peroneal nerve supplies the anterior compartment dorsiflexors, extensor digitorum brevis, first two dorsal interossei and the first web space.

Common peroneal injury causes weak dorsiflexion/foot drop, loss of eversion, loss of toe extension, and sensory loss over the anterolateral leg and dorsum of the foot.

candidates.subject: Anatomy
candidates.value:
Bone mainly contains type 1 collagen fibres. Bones are made up of mineralized collagenous extracellular matrix around specialized cells.

The extracellular matrix is composed of: organic component—around 30% of the organic matrix of bone is made up of collagen, mainly type 1 collagen; inorganic component—the major inorganic mineral in the bone matrix is calcium phosphate in the form of microcrystalline hydroxyapatite.

The specialized cells are: osteoblasts—responsible for synthesis, deposition, and mineralization of bone matrix; collagen is synthesized in bone by osteoblasts and osteoblasts become osteocytes after embedding in matrix. Osteocytes are the major cell type of mature bone, distributed throughout the matrix, and have lost the ability to divide or secrete new matrix. Osteoclasts are responsible for local removal of bone during bone growth and remodelling.

The clavicle is a modified long bone, as it has a modified shaft and no medullary cavity.

Typical long bones have an elongated shaft (diaphysis) and two expanded ends (epiphysis); the shaft has a central medullary cavity and a nutrient foramen directed away from the growing end. Examples include humerus, ulna, radius, femur, tibia and fibula.

candidates.subject: Anatomy
candidates.value:
The Haversian system is seen in compact bone, not cancellous bone.

Compact bones are composed of cylindrical structural units called Haversian systems or osteons. Each contains a central canal with small blood vessels, nerves and endosteum, surrounded by multiple lamellae of calcified matrix containing type I collagen fibres; these canals communicate through Volkmann's canals.

The lamellae of cancellous/spongy bone are arranged in a meshwork and do not form Haversian systems. The diaphysis and outer cortex of long bones are predominantly compact bone, while the epiphysis and inner medulla are predominantly cancellous bone.

The X-ray shows Codman's triangle, due to an irregular periosteal reaction commonly seen in osteosarcoma. The periosteum is a thick fibrous membrane covering the outer surface of all bones except joint surfaces and tendon/ligament insertion points (entheses). At the articular margin, the periosteum is continuous with the joint capsule.

The periosteum has two layers: outer fibrous layer containing fibroblasts; inner cambium/osteogenic layer containing progenitor cells that develop into osteoblasts. It is nourished by periosteal arteries and has a rich nerve supply, making it the most sensitive part of bone.

Frontal bones undergo intramembranous ossification; the other listed bones undergo enchondral ossification.

Hairpin bends of end arteries are seen abundantly in the metaphysis.

candidates.value: D-mannose and L-mannose are enantiomers. Enantiomers are mirror images of each other. The designation of a sugar isomer as the D- or L- form is determined by its spatial relationship to the parent compound of the carbohydrates, that is, the three-carbon sugar glyceraldehyde. The orientation of the —H and —OH groups around the penultimate carbon atom determines whether the sugar belongs to the D- or L- series. When the —OH group on the penultimate carbon atom of the sugar is on the right side, then the sugar is designated as a D- isomer. When the —OH group is on the left, it is an L-isomer. Naturally occurring monosaccharides are D-sugars and naturally occurring amino acids are L-isomers. Racemase enzyme interconverts between D and L isomers. Examples of enantiomers include D-glucose and L-glucose, D-fructose and L-fructose and D-mannose and L-mannose °. H ©. candidates.value: The galactose tolerance test is used to estimate liver function. Galactose is metabolized to glucose almost exclusively by the liver. Hence, the galactose tolerance test is done to assess the functional capacity of the liver. In liver dysfunction, galactose is excreted in the urine in increased amounts. The liver function is measured as the rate of excretion of galactose in urine following the ingestion or intravenous injection of a known amount of galactose. Normally, less than 3 g appear in the urine within 5 hours after the ingestion of 40 g of galactose.

candidates.value: Hyaluronic acid plays an important role in cellular migration. It is composed of repeating disaccharide units of N-acetyl glucosamine and glucuronic acid. It has no sulfate group. Hyaluronic acid is the only GAG that is not covalently attached to core protein. It is located in Synovial fluid, vitreous humor, the umbilical cord, cartilage. Heparan sulfate is a GAG made up of repeating units of glucosamine and glucuronic acid. candidates.value: The clinical features point to the diagnosis of Hurler's disease (MPS 1). Deficiency of the enzyme a-L-iduronidase that degrades glycosaminoglycans results in Hurler’s disease. Hurler’s disease was also known previously as gargoylism (coarse facial features). Clinical features of the disease include coarse facial features, corneal clouding, large tongue, and inguinal hernias. They also present with hepatosplenomegaly, short stature, skeletal dysplasia, and can present with hydrocephalus or valvular heart disease. These patients also have Reilly body inclusions in their leukocytes. The gene encoding o-L-iduronidase is present on chromosome 4. Heparan sulfate and dermatan sulfate are accumulated. Enzyme replacement therapy is available in the form of aldurazyme. Mucopolysaccharidoses are a group of metabolic disorders caused by the absence or malfunctioning of lysosomal enzymes needed to break down molecules called glycosaminoglycans. * Most common MPS: Sanfilippo > Hunter's and Hurler’s + MPS with no mental retardation: Scheie’s disease, Morquio syndrome, and Maroteaux—Lamy syndrome. + MPS with no corneal clouding: Hunter's disease and Sanfilippo syndrome + MPS with XLR inheritance: Hunter's disease + MPS with no visceromegaly: Morquio’s disease * Skeletal deformity associated with all MPS: Dysostosis multiplex * MPS with no leucocyte inclusions: Morquio’s disease

candidates.value: The given clinical scenario of a child with easy fatiguability, irritability, and inability to concentrate with the images showing a crumpled tissue paper appearance(Gaucher's cell) is suggestive of Gaucher's disease. The deficient enzyme is glucocerebrosidase (also known as beta-glucosidase). I Gaucher's disease is an inborn error of metabolism caused due to a deficiency of beta glucocerebrosidase. It is the most common lysosomal storage disorder and the mode of inheritance is autosomal recessive. There is an accumulation of lipid-laden macrophages in the spleen, liver, and other tissues. There are three clinical subtypes - type I (chronic non-neuronopathic), type II (acute neuronopathic), and type III (intermediate). Clinical features include anemia, thrombocytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, and neurological features depending on the subtype. Gaucher's cells - These are formed as a result of the accumulation of massive amounts of glucocerebrosides within the phagocytes. The cells have a fibrillary cytoplasm and give a crumpled tissue paper appearance. Option A: Deficiency of beta-hexosaminidase A is seen in Tay-Sachs disease. The deficiency of beta-hexosaminidase A and B causes Sandhoff's disease. Clinical features are seizures, macrocephaly, and hyperacusis. Option C: Deficiency of sphingomyelinase leads to Niemann-Pick disease. It is characterized by the presence of foam cells in the bone marrow. There may be pulmonary infiltrates leading to lung failure. Option D: Deficiency of N-acetylglucosaminidase leads to Sanfillipo's disease. It is a type of mucopolysaccharidosis (MPS - III). There is an accumulation of heparan sulfate leading to severe cognitive degeneration. “i ae a & w kK “oO fa" . CC

candidates.value: GLUT 4 is the glucose transporter in the myocytes under the influence of insulin. Glucose transport in the body mainly occurs through sodium-independent glucose transporters, which include GLUT transporters and, to a small extent, sodium-dependent glucose transporters present in the small intestine. Insulin induces movement of intracellular GLUT 4 molecules to the cell surface and thus increases glucose uptake. In type 2 diabetes mellitus, membrane GLUT 4 is reduced, leading to insulin resistance in muscle and fat cells.

candidates.subject: Biochemistry
candidates.value: Glucose is the only cellular substrate that can be phosphorylated by glucokinase. Glucokinase has a higher Vmax and higher Km value than hexokinase, requiring a higher concentration of glucose for half saturation. Hence glucokinase functions only when intracellular glucose concentration is high, as immediately after a carbohydrate-rich meal. Compared with hexokinase: glucokinase is in liver and pancreatic beta cells, has high Km and high Vmax, is not inhibited by G6P, and is inducible. Hexokinase is in most tissues, has low Km and low Vmax, is inhibited by G6P, and is not inducible. The source notes that glucokinase can act on other hexoses such as fructose and mannose, but because its Km for these reactions is high, this is not significant; therefore the best option has been chosen as given in the source answer key.

candidates.subject: Biochemistry
candidates.chapter: Glycogen metabolism and glycogen storage disorders
candidates.value: Breakdown of glycogen under anaerobic conditions yields 3 ATPs. Breakdown of glycogen yields glucose-6-phosphate which can enter the glycolysis pathway. Since it bypasses the first step, one ATP is saved and anaerobic glycolysis yields 3 ATPs. The first step in glycolysis involves conversion of glucose to glucose-6-phosphate and requires one ATP. Glycogen breakdown leads directly to glucose-6-phosphate, thereby bypassing this ATP-requiring step. One ATP is used for conversion of fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate. Net ATP formed from anaerobic glycolysis of glycogen is therefore 3 ATP.

candidates.value: Pompe's disease is the glycogen storage disease (GSD) that is also a lysosomal storage disorder. A small amount of glycogen is degraded by the lysosomal enzyme α(1→4)-glucosidase, also known as acid maltase. Deficiency of this enzyme causes accumulation of glycogen in vacuoles in lysosomes and is called type II GSD or Pompe's disease. candidates.value: The clinical symptoms of hypotonia, hepatomegaly, and cardiomegaly, along with muscle biopsy showing vacuoles are suggestive of Pompe's disease. Pompe's disease (type II glycogen storage disorder) occurs due to a mutation in alpha-1,4-glucosidase (also known as acid maltase), a lysosomal enzyme. Clinical features include hypotonia (floppy baby syndrome), cardiomyopathy, hepatomegaly, and failure to thrive. candidates.subject: Biochemistry
candidates.chapter: Glycogen metabolism and glycogen storage disorders
candidates.value: Von Gierke’s disease is inherited as an autosomal recessive trait. Von Gierke disease (type I glycogen storage disorder) occurs due to the deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase enzyme in the liver, kidney, and intestinal mucosa. Patients present commonly by 3-4 months of age with hypoglycemia (leading to seizures), lactic acidosis, and hepatomegaly. Affected children often have a doll-like face with fat cheeks, relatively thin extremities, short stature, and a protuberant abdomen due to massive hepatomegaly. The kidneys are also enlarged, whereas the spleen and heart are not involved. Laboratory findings include hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, and hyperlipidemia.

candidates.value: The non-oxidative phase of the HMP pathway is reversible. In the HMP shunt, no ATP is formed, but formation of NADPH and ribose takes place. The pentose phosphate pathway is an alternative route for the metabolism of glucose. It does not lead to formation of ATP, but its two major functions are: main source of NADPH, important for reductive biosynthesis of fatty acids and steroids and maintenance of reduced glutathione for antioxidant activity; and synthesis of ribose-5-phosphate. There are two phases in the HMP pathway: oxidative—irreversible, and non-oxidative—reversible.

candidates.value: The most likely diagnosis is glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. The clinical features are suggestive of an acute hemolytic reaction following administration of cotrimoxazole. A hemolytic attack starts with abrupt onset of malaise, weakness, and abdominal or lumbar pain. After an interval of several hours to 2–3 days, the patient develops jaundice and often dark urine due to hemoglobinuria. The peripheral smear shows characteristic bite cells or degmacytes/blister cells. In G6PD deficiency, uncontrolled oxidative stress causes hemoglobin denaturation and formation of Heinz bodies; bite cells result from removal of Heinz bodies by macrophages in the spleen. Cotrimoxazole contains sulfamethoxazole, which triggers a hemolytic reaction in persons with G6PD deficiency.

candidates.subject: Biochemistry
candidates.value:
Pyruvate kinase is not a component of the pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) enzyme complex.

PDH is a multienzyme complex associated with the inner mitochondrial membrane and catalyzes oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA.

The three enzyme components are:
• Pyruvate dehydrogenase
• Dihydrolipoyl transacetylase
• Dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase

The cofactors are:
• Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP)
• Lipoic acid
• Coenzyme A
• FAD
• NAD+

Overall reaction: Pyruvate + NAD+ + CoA → Acetyl-CoA + NADH + H+ + CO2.

Clinical aspects:
• Arsenite and mercuric ions react with -SH groups of lipoic acid and inhibit pyruvate dehydrogenase.
• Dietary thiamine deficiency inhibits PDH; chronic alcoholics may develop potentially fatal pyruvic and lactic acidosis.
• Inherited pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency presents with lactic acidosis, particularly after a glucose load, and neurological disturbances.

Note: Pyruvate kinase catalyzes the last step of glycolysis, transferring phosphate from phosphoenolpyruvate to ADP to form pyruvate and ATP.

Conversion of pyruvate to oxaloacetate is an anaplerotic reaction, catalyzed by pyruvate carboxylase.

Anaplerotic reactions form intermediates of a metabolic pathway. This reaction is important in maintaining an adequate concentration of oxaloacetate for condensation with acetyl-CoA. If acetyl-CoA accumulates, it activates pyruvate carboxylase and inhibits pyruvate dehydrogenase, ensuring an adequate supply of oxaloacetate.

Other anaplerotic reactions:
• Compounds yielding propionyl CoA can be carboxylated and isomerized to succinyl CoA.
• Glutamate and glutamine yield alpha-ketoglutarate via glutaminase and glutamate dehydrogenase reactions.
• Transamination of aspartate leads directly to formation of oxaloacetate.

Alanine is extracted by the liver and undergoes transamination with alpha-ketoglutarate by alanine transaminase (ALT) to form pyruvate and glutamate. Pyruvate is in turn converted to glucose by gluconeogenesis and glucose is released into the blood.

This child presents with diarrhea, dermatitis, and delayed mental development. This combined with neutral aminoaciduria and a positive Obermeyer test should raise suspicions of Hartnup’s disease. This is due to impaired renal and intestinal absorption of tryptophan and other neutral amino acids.
Hartnup’s disease is characterized by a varied clinical presentation including ataxia (lack of muscle control), delayed mental development, diarrhea, and dermatitis. Patients can also develop symptoms similar to pellagra as tryptophan is a precursor of niacin.
Diagnosis is based on aminoaciduria and increased excretion of indole compounds detected by Obermeyer test.

The image shows hexagonal, translucent, white crystals suggestive of cystinuria. Histidine is not seen in the urine of this patient.
Cystinuria is an autosomal-recessive disease due to a defect in renal PCT and intestinal amino acid transport that is essential for reabsorptive transport of cystine and the dibasic amino acids Ornithine, Lysine, and Arginine (COLA).
Diagnosis of cystinuria is by the cyanide-nitroprusside test. Initial treatment is with adequate hydration, alkalization of the urine with citrate supplementation or acetazolamide, and dietary modification to reduce salt and protein intake. If this fails then patients are usually started on chelation therapy with penicillamine.

candidates.subject: Biochemistry
candidates.value:
This child presented with an acute stroke. This in addition to elongated limbs and a tall body habitus with ocular examination showing downward subluxation of the lens is suggestive of homocystinuria.
Homocystinuria is an important cause of pediatric stroke. It is most commonly caused by a defect in cystathionine β synthase enzyme leading to homocysteine accumulation in the urine and blood. They are generally normal at birth; the first sign usually is subluxation of the lens (ectopia lentis) seen after 3 years of age.
Manifestations of homocystinuria:
• Ectopia lentis
• Intellectual disability and psychiatric and behavioral disorders
• Thromboembolic episodes
• Skeletal abnormalities resembling those of Marfan syndrome: they are tall and thin with elongated limbs and arachnodactyly
Elevations of both methionine and homocysteine in body fluids are the diagnostic lab findings.
Note: Marfan syndrome is the other cause of heritable ectopia lentis. However, in Marfan’s, the lens is dislocated in an upward and temporal direction whereas in homocystinuria the lens is dislocated in a downward and nasal direction.

The main defect in primary hyperoxaluria type I is the deficiency of the alanine glyoxylate aminotransferase in liver peroxisomes causing failure to catabolize glyoxylate formed by the deamination of glycine. Plasma levels of ornithine are elevated in gyrate atrophy of the retina and choroid.
The initial reactions in arginine catabolism are the conversion of arginine to ornithine followed by the transamination of ornithine. Any mutation in ornithine aminotransferase leads to elevated plasma and urinary concentrations of ornithine. This is associated with a condition known as gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina. It presents with myopia and night blindness in adolescence which progresses to legal blindness by 50 years. The condition is treated with dietary restriction of arginine.

Boiled cabbage odor in urine, sweat, and breath occurs in hypermethioninemia. Dimethylsulphide, a metabolite of methionine, causes the characteristic boiled cabbage smell.
People with a genetic deficiency of α/β-methionine adenosyltransferase present with hypermethioninemia and neural demyelination. However, they’re usually asymptomatic until early adulthood.
Methionine adenosyltransferase converts methionine to S-adenosyl Methionine (SAM), a principal methyl donor. Hence the enzyme deficiency causes excess accumulation of methionine and its breakdown metabolites.

candidates.value:
A fishy odor is seen in trimethylaminuria. Consumption of food products with choline should be avoided in fish odor syndrome.
Fish odor syndrome (trimethylaminuria) is an autosomal recessive disease where TMA (trimethylamine) is not converted to the non-odorous TMAO (TMA-N-oxide) in the liver. This is due to the deficiency of flavin-containing mono oxygenase 3 (FMO3). TMA then builds up in the body and is released in sweat, urine, and breath, giving off a strong odor of rotting fish from the body.
Choline, lecithin, and TMAO are precursors of trimethylamine which are found in food products. These food products are eggs, liver, peanuts, meat, poultry, fish, dairy foods, pasta, and rice.

candidates.subject: Biochemistry
candidates.value:
Urinary levels of 3-methylhistidine are decreased in patients with Wilson disease.
Amino acids in urine exist either in conjugated form (most) or in free form. In Wilson's disease the amount of conjugated amino acids far exceeds the amount of free amino acids. Methyl histidine largely exists in free form and does not increase in amount on hydrolysis of acids in urine. Hence low amounts is seen in Wilson's disease.
Wilson disease is an autosomal-recessive disorder caused by mutation of the ATP7B gene located on chromosome 13. The ATP7B gene encodes a transmembrane copper-transporting ATPase expressed on the hepatocyte canalicular membrane.
Deficiency in the ATP7B protein causes a decrease in copper excretion into the bile, impairs its incorporation into ceruloplasmin, and inhibits ceruloplasmin secretion into the blood, leading to the accumulation of toxic levels of copper in the liver, brain, and eye.

candidates.subject: Biochemistry
candidates.value:
Urine turning black on exposure to air is suggestive of alkaptonuria which occurs due to the defect in homogentisate oxidase enzyme.
Alkaptonuria is a disorder of tyrosine metabolism, that develops due to the defect in homogentisate oxidase, which oxidizes homogentisate to maleylacetoacetate. The defect in this enzyme leads to the accumulation of homogentisate, which is then excreted in the urine. The excreted homogentisate gets oxidized when exposed to air and causes the urine to turn black.
In some cases, the excessive homogentisate may get oxidized to benzoquinone acetate, which binds to the connective tissue. This leads to arthritis and pigmentation of the connective tissue, a condition called ochronosis.
Other options:
Option B: Xanthine oxidase deficiency results in hypouricemia, xanthinuria, and xanthine lithiasis.
Option C: Defects in phenylalanine hydroxylase can lead to phenylketonuria characterised by hyperreflexia, seizures, hypopigmentation, low IQ, hyperactivity, and tremors.
Option D: Defects in dihydroorotate dehydrogenase are rarely seen in clinical practice. Miller syndrome is associated with this defect.

candidates.value:
This child with vomiting, lethargy, and irritability with an X-linked recessive urea cycle disorder most likely has hyperammonemia type II.

Hyperammonemia type II is due to the deficiency of the enzyme ornithine transcarbamoylase. It is the most frequent urea cycle defect. Biochemical findings include elevated levels of glutamine in the blood, urine, CSF, low citrulline, and high urinary orotic acid. This condition may be precipitated by a switch from formula to whole milk.

Urea cycle disorders are all characterized by hyperammonemia, encephalopathy, and respiratory alkalosis. There is an accumulation of the precursors of urea - ammonia, and glutamine. They include:
• Defect in carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I - Hyperammonemia type 1
• Defect in ornithine transcarbamoylase - Hyperammonemia type 2
• Defect in argininosuccinate synthetase - Citrullinemia
• Defect in argininosuccinate lyase - Argininosuccinic aciduria
• Defect in the gene for arginase - Hyperargininemia

Clinical features of urea cycle disorders are common to all and include vomiting, avoidance of high-protein foods, intermittent ataxia, irritability, lethargy, and severe mental retardation.

Note: Classically, Type 2 Hyperammonemia is an X-linked recessive disorder. But in certain heterozygous females (with one mutated gene), the disease manifests and they necessarily do not remain as carriers. In them, the disease follows an X-linked partially dominant pattern of inheritance.

candidates.subject: Biochemistry
candidates.value:
This infant with failure to thrive, hypoglycemia, elevated levels of glutamine and uracil levels most likely has hyperammonemia type 2. This condition occurs due to the deficiency of the enzyme ornithine transcarbamoylase.

There is an accumulation of carbamoyl phosphate, which then enters into pyrimidine synthesis producing orotic acid and uracil and leading to orotic aciduria and high uracil in blood and urine. Since the ammonia from glutamine is not converted into urea, its level increases. Glutamate is not regenerated. Since glutamate is not available for transamination, amino acids cannot be used for gluconeogenesis. Hence, the glucose level drops in the blood.

Treatment:
• Reducing intake of ammonia - Dietary protein, a metabolic source of ammonium, is restricted and caloric intake is provided by glucose and fat.
• Increasing excretion of ammonia - Addition of phenylbutyrate, which scavenges nitrogen by combining with amino acids to form a more water-soluble product. This can be easily excreted by the kidneys.

candidates.value:
Omega 3 (ω3) fatty acids have anti-inflammatory effects.

ω3 fatty acids, such as linolenic, eicosapentaenoic and docosahexaenoic acids, result in synthesis of less inflammatory prostaglandins and leukotrienes. This contributes to their anti-inflammatory effect. They also have anti-thrombotic effects. This is because thromboxane A3 (formed from ω3 fatty acids) is less thrombogenic than thromboxane A2 (formed from ω6 fatty acids). ω3 fatty acids have also been shown to reduce serum triglyceride levels.

Linoleic acid and α-linolenic acid are essential fatty acids.

Essential fatty acids refer to polyunsaturated fatty acids(PUFAs) required for biological processes which are not synthesized by the body. Thus, they must be acquired from diet. The two essential fatty acids in humans are linoleic acid (Omega 6) - the precursor of arachidonic acid - and α-Linolenic acid (Omega 3) - the precursor of eicosapentaenoic acid and docosahexaenoic acid. Arachidonic acid and γ-Linolenic acid are semi-essential fatty acids since they can be derived from essential fatty acids.

Dry skin, scaly rash, hair loss and poor wound healing with malabsorption syndrome are suggestive of essential fatty acid deficiency due to malabsorption. Linoleic acid is an essential fatty acid.

Essential fatty acids (Linoleic acid and α-Linolenic acid) are needed for many physiologic processes, including maintaining the integrity of skin and cell membranes. Deficiency of essential fatty acid is a rarely seen clinical entity in healthy adults and children who consume a varied diet. However, it can occur in individuals with risk factors affecting fatty acid absorption, like cystic fibrosis, pancreatic insufficiency, inflammatory bowel disease, massive bowel resection and prolonged parenteral nutrition. Patients with essential fatty acids deficiency have loss of structural integrity of the cell membranes, leading to like scaly dermatitis, hair loss and poor wound healing.

Trans fatty acids are a by-product of the hydrogenation of vegetable oils.

Trans fatty acids are isomers of cis fatty acids, the naturally occurring unsaturated fatty acids. The configuration of groups in a trans fatty acid is such that the acyl chains are on the opposite side of the double bond. They are formed during the hydrogenation of vegetable oils and in the production of margarine.

Trans fatty acids raise the level of triglycerides, total and LDL cholesterol and also lower the level of HDL. Hence their consumption is associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular disease. WHO recommends that the intake of trans fats should be less than 1% of the total energy intake.

candidates.subject: Biochemistry
candidates.value:
A young boy with muscle aches, hypotonia, poor exercise tolerance, myoglobinuria and elevated creatine kinase suggests a deficiency of carnitine.

Carnitine is a key transporter needed for beta-oxidation of fatty acids. It binds to acyl-CoAs to form acylcarnitine. This helps in the transfer of fatty acids across the impermeable inner mitochondrial membrane for beta-oxidation. Thus, carnitine deficiency results in impaired beta-oxidation of fatty acids. There will be inadequate ATP production in response to increased demands (e.g. exercise) with excess fatty acid accumulation in muscle cells. This results in muscle breakdown.

Patients with carnitine deficiency present with hypoglycemia, muscle aches, hypotonia and poor exercise tolerance (myopathy). They have high levels of serum creatine kinase. Treatment includes carnitine supplementation.

Very long-chain fatty acids are accumulated in cerebrohepatorenal syndrome.

Cerebrohepatorenal syndrome, also known as Zellweger's syndrome, is a rare inherited disorder characterised by the absence of peroxisomes in all tissues. It is caused by mutations in the genes encoding peroxins, which take part in peroxisome biosynthesis. There is accumulation of C26-C38 polyenoic acids in brain tissues along with generalised loss of peroxisomal functions. Patients present with severe neurological symptoms and most die within a year. Other biochemical findings include abnormalities in the bile acid synthesis and a decreased plasmalogens.

candidates.subject: Biochemistry
candidates.value:
'Propionyl CoA is produced by the oxidation of odd-chain fatty acids' is the correct statement.

In the oxidation of odd-chain fatty acids, the last cycle of oxidation yields a three-carbon-containing propionyl CoA. Propionyl CoA is carboxylated to methylmalonyl CoA by propionyl CoA carboxylase, a biotin-dependent enzyme that requires ATP hydrolysis.

Methylmalonyl CoA is further converted into succinyl CoA by racemase and mutase, (a vitamin B12 dependent enzyme) which enters into the TCA cycle.Thus, propionyl CoA can be converted into glucose by gluconeogenesis.

Note:
• Methylmalonyl CoA mutase is a vitamin B12-dependent enzyme.
• Propionyl residue from an odd-chain fatty acid is the only part of a fatty acid that is glucogenic.

In the β-oxidation of palmitic acid (C16), 8 molecules of acetyl-CoA are produced.

In the beta-oxidation pathway, two carbons at a time are cleaved from acyl-CoA molecules between alpha(2) and beta(3) carbons, starting at the carboxyl end. The two-carbon units formed are called acetyl-CoA.

candidates.subject: Biochemistry
candidates.value:
Carnitine palmitoyl transferase-1 (CPT-1), is the rate-limiting enzyme in the beta-oxidation of fatty acids.

CPT-1 is responsible for transferring the acyl group from CoA to carnitine, forming acylcarnitine which can enter the outer mitochondrial membrane. Thus the acyl group enters the mitochondria from the cytoplasm.

Malonyl CoA is an inhibitor of CPT-1. Thus,
• In the fed state, with high insulin: glucagon ratio, acetyl CoA carboxylase is active and malonyl CoA is produced, which inhibits β-oxidation.
• In the fasting state, with low insulin: glucagon ratio, acetyl CoA carboxylase is inactive and malonyl CoA is not produced. Hence, β-oxidation takes place.

A deficiency of fetal long-chain 3-hydroxy acyl CoA dehydrogenase (LCHAD) is involved in the pathogenesis of acute fatty liver of pregnancy.

Free fatty acids normally increase in pregnancy, particularly during late gestation to fuel fetoplacental growth and development. In fetuses homozygous for LCHAD deficiency, the fetoplacental unit is unable to undertake fatty acid metabolism adequately. This contributes to the accumulation of long-chain metabolites in maternal blood and hepatocytes, resulting in toxic effects.

The given clinical vignette is suggestive of medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency in which there is impaired beta-oxidation of medium-chain fatty acids. This leads to the accumulation of dicarboxylic acids leading to dicarboxylic aciduria. It is characterized by:
• Excretion of C6-C10 ω-dicarboxylic acids (medium-chain) in the urine.
• Nonketotic hypoglycemia: due to the lack of ATP and acetyl CoA from β-oxidation (which is an activator of pyruvate carboxylase) to support gluconeogenesis.

Defects in medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase have been identified as a cause of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS).

Omega-oxidation is an alternative way of fatty acid oxidation in the body when the beta-oxidation enzymes are either saturated or defective. Omega oxidation converts excess fatty acids to dicarboxylic acids that are soluble and hence can be excreted out via urine.

• Brush field spots

Acetoacetate is a primary ketone body as it is directly synthesized by the pathway of ketogenesis.

Secondary ketone bodies are those which are produced from the primary ketone body via spontaneous breakdown or by enzymatic reaction. Examples of secondary ketone bodies are: acetone and beta-hydroxybutyrate.

Ketone bodies are formed under conditions associated with a high rate of fatty acid oxidation such as:
• Fasting
• Carbohydrate restrictive diet
• Starvation
• Prolonged intense exercise
• Untreated (or inadequately treated) type 1 diabetes mellitus.

In such conditions, there is increased production of acetyl CoA from beta-oxidation of fatty acids which inhibits pyruvate dehydrogenase and activates pyruvate carboxylase. The oxaloacetate thus produced is used for gluconeogenesis rather than the TCA cycle. Hence, acetyl CoA is diverted into ketone body synthesis.

Thus, acetoacetate is the primary ketone body synthesized.

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of diabetic ketoacidosis which is an insulin-deficient state leading to increased lipid breakdown (lipolysis) into fatty acids. This condition is also characterized by hyperglycemia and increased ketone body synthesis.

Type 1 diabetes mellitus is commonly found in the adolescent population. In response to certain precipitating factors, such patients may develop a severe insulin-deficient state. Since insulin is an inhibitor of hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL), an insulin-deficient state will cause HSL overactivity in adipocytes and the breakdown of lipid into fatty acids (lipolysis). A fruity smell (presence of acetone in breath) and positive ketostix test (ketonuria) on the background of prolonged starvation is suggestive of starvation ketosis. This is characterized by increased activity of HMG CoA synthase enzyme.

candidates.subject: Biochemistry
candidates.value:
The liver cannot utilize ketone bodies.

The ketone bodies synthesized in the liver mitochondria are transported in the blood to the peripheral tissues, where they are utilized by the following steps:
• β-hydroxybutyrate is oxidized to acetoacetate by β-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase producing NADH.
• Acetoacetate is then activated to acetoacetyl CoA by transferring a CoA molecule from succinyl CoA by succinyl CoA-acetoacetate CoA transferase (thiophorase).
• Acetoacetyl CoA is cleaved into two acetyl CoA molecules by thiolase and oxidized into CO2 by the TCA cycle.

RBCs cannot utilize ketone bodies as they lack mitochondria.

The liver cannot utilize ketone bodies as it lacks the enzyme thiophorase.

candidates.subject: Biochemistry
candidates.chapter: Biosynthesis of fatty acids and Eicosanoids
candidates.value:
The reducing equivalent for fatty acid synthesis in the liver is NADPH. The most important source of NADPH is the hexose monophosphate shunt (HMP) pathway.

The HMP shunt pathway, or pentose phosphate pathway, is an alternative route for the metabolism of glucose. It generates NADPH and synthesizes ribose. NADP+ is hydrogenated to NADPH by glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase. Since the HMP shunt pathway and de novo fatty acid synthesis both occur in the cytosol of the cell, there are no membranes or permeability barriers against the transfer of NADPH. Thus, this forms the major source for NADPH for fatty acid synthesis.

Other minor sources of NADPH are extramitochondrial isocitrate dehydrogenase and NADP malate dehydrogenase (malic enzyme).

Citrate is an allosteric activator of acetyl-CoA carboxylase.

Acetyl-CoA carboxylase is the rate-limiting enzyme in de novo fatty acid synthesis. Citrate promotes the conversion of acetyl CoA carboxylase from an inactive dimer to an active polymeric form. candidates.chapter: Biosynthesis of fatty acids and Eicosanoids
candidates.value:
The restoration of fat storage in a child undergoing nutritional rehabilitation, as evidenced by adequate weight gain and an increase in subcutaneous body fat, occurs with the help of acetyl CoA carboxylase.

With appropriate supplementation of nutrition, the child's body will gradually enter an anabolic phase. In the well fed state, there is an abundant supply of glucose, which is converted to pyruvate, which in turn is converted to acetyl CoA. Acetyl CoA is diverted into fatty acid synthesis, in which acetyl CoA carboxylase is the rate-limiting enzyme. There is also a high insulin : glucagon ratio in the well fed state. This favors dephosphorylation (activation) of acetyl CoA carboxylase, resulting in increased fatty acid synthesis. The fatty acids thus formed (most commonly palmitoyl CoA) are esterified into triacylglycerols. This process is called lipogenesis.

Note: The enzymes acyl-CoA dehydrogenase, thiolase, and carnitine palmitoyl transferase-I are involved in fatty acid oxidation and are inactive in the well-fed state.

candidates.subject: Biochemistry
candidates.chapter: Biosynthesis of fatty acids and Eicosanoids
candidates.value:
Malonyl-CoA is the most active donor of two carbon atoms in fatty acid synthesis.

Malonyl-CoA is a 3-carbon unit that donates 2 carbon units in fatty acid synthesis. It is formed from acetyl-CoA by acetyl-CoA carboxylase. During fatty acid synthesis, acetyl CoA primarily acts as the primer. The enzyme fatty acid synthase (FAS) adds two carbons from malonyl-CoA to the initial acetyl-CoA, forming a 4-carbon intermediate (butyryl-ACP). FAS then sequentially adds two carbons from malonyl-CoA to the ACP-intermediates (eg: butyryl-ACP) to elongate the fatty acid chain.

Thus, in the end product palmitic acid (C16), only carbon atoms 15 and 16 are from acetyl CoA. The remaining 14 carbon atoms are derived from malonyl-CoA. Thus, malonyl-CoA is the most active donor of two carbon atoms in fatty acid synthesis.

Note:
Option 3: Fatty acid synthesis is not a simple reversal of oxidation of fatty acids. These two processes involve completely different enzymes and occur in different compartments of the cell.
Option 4: Intermediates in fatty acid synthesis are covalently linked to the sulfhydryl group of an acyl carrier protein (ACP), not coenzyme A, of the enzyme fatty acid synthase. Intermediates in the fatty acid breakdown are covalently attached to the sulfhydryl group of coenzyme A.

Sudden onset of severe breathlessness and wheezing with a reduced peak expiratory flow rate is suggestive of acute exacerbation of asthma. 5-lipoxygenase enzyme is important for the pathogenesis of this condition.

Acute exacerbation of asthma is characterized by bronchoconstriction due to chemicals mediators like leukotrienes (LTB4, LTC4, LTD4 etc.). Leukotrienes are produced from the breakdown of arachidonic acid by 5-lipoxygenase via the lipoxygenase pathway.

Leukotrienes also cause increased vascular permeability and activation and attraction of leukocytes. Thus, they are involved in many inflammatory or immediate hypersensitivity reactions, such as asthma.

Chronic fatigue, growth retardation, epistaxis, hepatosplenomegaly, thrombocytopenia, anemia, Erlenmeyer flask deformity of femur with bone marrow biopsy showing cells with wrinkled tissue paper appearance suggest Gaucher’s disease.

Gaucher's disease is a genetic disorder in which glucocerebroside accumulates in the reticuloendothelial system due to the deficiency of the enzyme glucocerebrosidase (acid β-glucosidase). It is the most common lysosomal storage disorder.

Affected children present with bleeding tendencies secondary to thrombocytopenia, chronic fatigue secondary to anemia, painless hepatomegaly and splenomegaly, and bone pain. They may have liver cirrhosis, osteoporosis and pathological fractures. Neurological symptoms such as developmental delay, hypertonia, strabismus, supranuclear gaze palsy are seen in type 3 Gaucher's disease. On bone marrow biopsy, Gaucher's cells with wrinkled tissue paper appearance are seen. Erlenmeyer flask deformity is seen on X-ray of femur.

Treatment is with enzyme replacement therapy in the form of human recombinant acid β-glucosidase (Imiglucerase), velaglucerase alfa or taliglucerase alfa.

Note: Neurological involvement is not seen in type I Gaucher's disease

candidates.subject: Biochemistry
candidates.value:
Cholesterol synthesis takes place in the cytosol and endoplasmic reticulum.

Cytosolic acetyl-CoA forms acetoacetyl-CoA, which condenses with another acetyl-CoA to form HMG-CoA.

Cytosolic HMG-CoA, a key intermediate in cholesterol biosynthesis, is reduced in the endoplasmic reticulum to mevalonic acid by the regulatory enzyme HMG-CoA reductase. Mevalonic acid subsequently undergoes phosphorylation, decarboxylation, condensation and cyclization reactions to produce cholesterol.

Summary of cholesterol synthesis pathway:
• Synthesis of mevalonate from acetyl-CoA
• Formation of isoprenoid units from mevalonate
• Condensation of six isoprenoid units form squalene
• Cyclization of squalene to give rise to the parent steroid, lanosterol
• Formation of cholesterol from lanosterol.

All tissues containing nucleated cells are capable of cholesterol synthesis, with the majority produced in the liver and intestine.

This reaction is catalyzed by the enzyme 7α-hydroxylase, a microsomal CYP450 enzyme, which requires NADPH, oxygen, and vitamin C as co-factors. It is the rate-limiting step in the synthesis of bile acids.

Regulation of bile acid synthesis occurs by feedback inhibition of 7α-hydroxylase via the Farnesoid X receptor. When the level of bile acids in the enterohepatic circulation increases, FXR is activated and transcription of the enzyme is suppressed.

candidates.value:
After a fatty meal, chylomicrons are elevated in lipoprotein lipase deficiency.

Chylomicrons transport dietary lipids from the intestine to the peripheral tissues. They are synthesized in the intestine by assembling apo B-48 with lipids (mainly triacylglycerols). This is called a nascent chylomicron, which upon receiving apo C-II and apo E from HDL is remodelled into mature chylomicron.

Apo C-II activates lipoprotein lipase present on the endothelium. Lipoprotein lipase hydrolyzes the triacylglycerols into fatty acids and glycerol which are either used for storage or energy. Therefore, patients who are deficient in lipoprotein lipase or apo C-II (type I hyperlipoproteinemia) show increased levels of chylomicrons in the plasma after a fatty meal.

The catalytic efficiency of an enzyme is expressed as Kcat/Km.

Kcat is the rate constant, which is the limiting rate of an enzyme-catalyzed reaction at saturation.
It is given by Vmax divided by number of active sites of the enzyme. Km is the
Michaelis-Menten constant, which is defined as the substrate concentration at which the initial
velocity(Vi) is half the maximum velocity (Vmax/2).

For some enzymes, when a substrate (S) binds to the active site of the enzyme (E), and forms an
enzyme-substrate complex (ES), the product is instantaneously formed. For such enzymes, the
reaction of E+S° ES becomes the rate-limiting step. Its rate is determined on the rate of diffusion
of the molecules in a solution. Hence, these enzymes are called diffusion-limited or

catalytically perfect.

Basal metabolic rate (BMR) is closely dependent on lean body mass (fat-free mass).
Lean body mass is the difference between total body weight and body fat weight. It is the metabolically active tissue in the body.
The BMR decreases with increasing age, even when body weight remains constant. This is the result of muscle tissue replacement by adipose tissue, which is metabolically less active. Women have a significantly lower BMR than men of the same body weight and age. This is because women’s bodies contain proportionally more adipose tissue.

This patient with difficult dark vision and gritty sensations in the eye with findings of soft corneas suggests vitamin A deficiency. In the retina, a form of vitamin A called retinal (11-cis retinaldehyde) plays an important role in Wald's visual cycle. Its deficiency leads to vision defects.
Rhodopsin, the visual pigment of the rod cells in the retina, consists of 11-cis retinal specifically bound to the protein opsin. When rhodopsin is exposed to light, a series of photochemical isomerizations occurs. This results in the bleaching of the visual pigment and release of all-trans-retinal and opsin. This process triggers a nerve impulse that is transmitted by the optic nerve to the brain.

The first hydroxylation of vitamin D takes place in the liver to form 25-hydroxycholecalciferol.
Vitamin D, as either cholecalciferol or ergocalciferol does not have significant biological activity. It is activated in the following steps:
Skin: 7-Dehydrocholesterol (an intermediate in the synthesis of cholesterol in the skin) undergoes a nonenzymic reaction on exposure to ultraviolet light (290nm to 315nm), yielding cholecalciferol.
Liver: Cholecalciferol is hydroxylated to 25-hydroxycholecalciferol (the most abundant circulatory form of Vitamin D) by the enzyme 25-hydroxylase.
Kidney: 25-hydroxycholecalciferol is converted to 1,25 dihydroxycholecalciferol (calcitriol), the biologically active form by the enzyme 1α-hydroxylase.
Calcitriol acts on the bone, intestine, and kidney to maintain calcium and phosphate homeostasis. If the body does not require vitamin D, in the kidney, 24-hydroxylase converts vitamin D into 24,25 dihydroxycholecalciferol, which is an inactive metabolite.

Decreased energy production is seen in thiamine deficiency because it acts as a coenzyme for pyruvate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase.
Both pyruvate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase are required for the production of NADH, which is used for ATP production. In thiamine deficiency, the reaction catalyzed by pyruvate dehydrogenase cannot go forward. Hence, there is no formation of acetyl CoA, causing decreased substrate for the citric acid cycle. As a result, energy (ATP) production is grossly reduced and instead, lactic acidosis is seen.
