Dry beriberi: Both the peripheral and central nervous systems are affected. Patients present with symmetric motor and sensory neuropathy (pain, paresthesia, loss of reflexes) especially in lower limbs. In severe cases, muscle atrophy may also be seen.

A patient with high intake of jowar and characteristic Casal’s necklace pattern rash is most likely suffering from pellagra. It is caused due to a deficiency of vitamin B3, known as niacin.

Pellagra is caused by niacin deficiency, either due to dietary deficiency or deficient conversion of tryptophan to niacin. Hence, pellagra-like symptoms are seen in:

Carcinoid syndrome: Due to excess conversion of tryptophan to serotonin, there is a decreased level of tryptophan available for niacin synthesis
Pyridoxine deficiency: Pyridoxine is required as the co-factor of kynureninase, an enzyme in the pathway of niacin synthesis.
Maize/corn rich diet: In these grans, niacin is in bound form (niacytin form) and is not absorbed.
Jowar diet (Sorghum): The increased leucine content inhibits QPRTase enzyme, an enzyme in the pathway of niacin synthesis.

An alcoholic patient with a red-colored beefy tongue, itching and the characteristic Casal's necklace, shown in the image, is suggestive of pellagra. It is caused by niacin/vitamin B3 deficiency. Hence, one should ask for a history of diarrhea and memory loss in this case.
Pellagra presents with 4 Ds: Diarrhea, Dermatitis, Dementia, and if untreated, Death. Early symptoms of pellagra are loss of appetite, generalized weakness and irritability, abdominal pain, and vomiting. Photosensitive dermatitis is seen over sun-exposed areas. Diarrhea occurs due to proctitis or malabsorption. Bright red glossitis (beefy tongue) and Casal’s necklace (a pigmented, scaly skin rash that forms a ring around the neck) follow. Depressive psychosis and dementia also commonly occur.
Corn/ maize/ jowar based diets are the main causes of niacin deficiency. Corn/maize lacks niacin and tryptophan. The excess leucine in jowar and maize disrupts the conversion of tryptophan to niacin. Niacin deficiency is also seen in alcoholism. Hence, additional histories of diarrhea and memory loss will aid in supporting the diagnosis of pellagra (along with dietary history).
Treatment includes oral supplementation with 100–200 mg of nicotinamide or nicotinic acid three times daily for 5 days.
Option B: Thiamine deficiency (vitamin B1) features include CVS manifestations like heart failure and edema (wet beriberi), peripheral neuritis (dry beriberi), and Wernicke encephalopathy (in alcoholics).
Option C: Dermatitis seen in pellagra is due to dietary deficiency of niacin and so allergy history is not relevant.
Option D: Conjunctivitis is not a feature of niacin deficiency.

candidates.subject: Biochemistry
candidates.value:
Niacin increases the level of HDL.
Niacin (vitamin B3) is known to inhibit lipolysis within the adipose tissue. Hence, the circulating free fatty acids (FFAs) are reduced. The liver normally uses these circulating FFAs as a precursor in the synthesis of triacylglycerol (TAG). As a result, niacin causes a reduction in liver TAG synthesis. TAGs are in turn required for very low density lipoprotein (VLDL) and low density lipoprotein (LDL) synthesis. Therefore both plasma VLDL and LDL values are reduced. Overall, niacin decreases LDL, VLDL and TAG levels, and increases high-density lipoprotein (HDL) levels. Thus it is particularly useful in the treatment of type IIb hyperlipoproteinemia, in which both VLDL and LDL are elevated.

candidates.value:
A 30-year-old patient who got his ileum removed due to Crohn's disease is likely to develop vitamin B12 deficiency. Vitamin B12 is absorbed from the distal third of the ileum via receptors known as cubulin, which binds the intrinsic factor-vitamin B12 complex.
Dietary vitamin B12 is normally bound to proteins in food. Pepsin and gastric acid in the stomach degrade these food proteins and release vitamin B12. The free vitamin B12 then binds to a salivary glycoprotein called haptocorrin (R-binder).
In the alkaline pH of the duodenum, pancreatic proteases degrade the haptocorrin, and vitamin B12 is released again. It then binds tightly to intrinsic factor (IF), a glycoprotein secreted by the parietal cells of the stomach and this binding takes place in the duodenum. The IF-Vitamin B12 complex reaches the terminal ileum and attaches to a receptor on the enterocyte, from where it is absorbed. Vitamin B12 is transported in the blood bound to a carrier protein called transcobalamin II and delivered to the peripheral tissues.
Absorption sites:
Iron- Duodenum
Folate- Jejunum
Vit B12- Ileum
[Figure: Absorption of vitamin B12 diagram showing dietary B12, R-protein/haptocorrin, intrinsic factor, pancreatic proteases, ileum and transcobalamin II.]

Folate trap occurs in the deficiency of vitamin B12.
[Figure: Methionine-Folate Cycle showing methionine synthase (vitamin B12), 5-methyl tetrahydrofolate, 5,10-methylene tetrahydrofolate, homocysteine and cystathionine β synthase (vitamin B6).]
The conversion of 5,10-methylene-THF into 5-methyl-THF(methyltetrahydrofolate) is an irreversible process. The major source of tetrahydrofolate for tissues is 5-methyl-THF. The only way to make further use of 5-methyl-THF and to maintain the folate cycle is by the vitamin B12-dependent remethylation of homocysteine to methionine by methionine synthase enzyme.
Decreased activity of methionine synthase in vitamin B12 deficiency results in the accumulation of methyltetrahydrofolate that cannot be used, resulting in a folate trap. The folate cycle provides a link between the functions of folate and vitamin B12, where vitamin B12 deficiency causes a functional deficiency of folate.

FOX (Ferrous oxidation in xylenol orange) assay

Lipid-engorged macrophages are killed by unesterified cholesterol.
Free radicals can damage the proteins and lipids in plasma low-density lipoprotein (LDL). They are chemically modified to form abnormal LDL which are not recognized by the liver LDL receptors. Thus, abnormal LDL is not cleared by the liver and is instead taken up by macrophage scavenger receptors. These lipid-engorged macrophages infiltrate the blood vessel endothelium. These macrophages are then killed by the high content of unesterified cholesterol they have accumulated. This causes the development of atherosclerotic plaques which, over time, can completely occlude a blood vessel.

NADPH + 2O2°  NADP+ + 2·O2− + 2H+

Nitric oxide can react with superoxide to yield peroxynitrite, which decays to form hydroxyl radicals
NADPH oxidase in the inflammatory cells produces superoxide

candidates.subject: Biochemistry
candidates.value:
Confusion and slurred speech with elevated blood ethanol levels suggests ethanol intoxication. The toxicity of ethanol is due to the increased NADH/NAD+ ratio.
Ethanol is metabolised in the liver by alcohol dehydrogenase. This reaction generates NADH. A high concentration of NADH leads to a high NADH/NAD+ ratio. Due to this, the metabolic reactions which require NAD+ are inhibited. This is the basic cause of all the metabolic effects of alcohol.
Glycolysis, citric acid cycle and fatty acid oxidation are inhibited. Ketogenesis is favoured. Pyruvate is shunted for lactate synthesis due to abundance of NADH and lactate/pyruvate ratio increases. Thus gluconeogenesis, which requires pyruvate as a substrate, is inhibited. This leads to hypoglycemia.

candidates.subject: Biochemistry
candidates.value:
In a patient with Menke's disease, glutathione peroxidase action is not affected.
Menke’s disease, or kinky/steely hair syndrome is an X-linked recessive condition, where there is a mutation in the ATP7A gene. This leads to defective copper-binding P-type ATPase and copper is not mobilized from the intestine. Thus copper deficiency occurs and enzymes containing copper are affected, like superoxide dismutase, dopamine hydroxylase and amine oxidase.
Glutathione peroxidase is not affected since it requires selenium in the form of selenocysteine.
Other copper deficiency disorders include Wilson’s disease and MEDNIK syndrome. Wilson’s disease is an autosomal recessive disorder, due to ATP7B mutation, a gene encoding for copper transporting ATPase in the cells. There is defective biliary copper excretion from liver cells, leading to copper deposits in the liver and brain. MEDNIK syndrome is a rare multisystem disorder of copper metabolism with features of both Wilson’s and Menke’s disease.
Note:
Other enzymes requiring copper are ferroxidase (ceruloplasmin) , cytochrome c oxidase, tyrosinase (melanin synthesis), lysyl oxidase (cross-linking in collagen). It is also a component of ferroportin, which is involved in iron absorption.

candidates.value:
Keshan disease is due to a deficiency of selenium.
Selenium is an important trace element that is a part of the 21st amino acid selenocysteine. There are many selenium-containing enzymes such as glutathione peroxidase, de-iodinase and thioredoxin reductase. Selenium is also an intracellular antioxidant that complements the role of vitamin E. Dietary sources of selenium include seafood, muscle meat, and some cereals.
Selenium deficiency leads to Keshan disease and Kashin-Beck disease. Keshan disease is an endemic cardiomyopathy found in children and young women residing in regions of China where dietary intake of selenium is low. Kashin-Beck disease is a chronic, endemic osteoarthropathy seen in regions of China and Russia.
Chronic ingestion of high amounts of selenium leads to selenosis or selenium toxicity. It is characterized by hair and nail brittleness, garlic breath odor, myopathy, irritability, and other abnormalities of the nervous system.

Calcium homeostasis: One-half of the total body magnesium is located in bone. Magnesium is important for parathormone secretion which controls serum Ca2+ level.
Neuromuscular function:
Hypomagnesemia may cause generalized alterations in neuromuscular function including tetany, tremor, seizures.
Hypermagnesemia is known to cause symptoms of neuromuscular blockade such as hypoactive tendon reflexes, GI hypomotility, paralysis.
Maintenance of cardiac rhythm:
Hypomagnesemia can lead to supraventricular and ventricular arrhythmias.
Hypermagnesemia can cause bradycardia, heart block, and asystole.
Magnesium deficiency symptoms are similar to those of calcium deficiency, but symptoms will be relieved only when magnesium is given. Oral administration of magnesium may lead to diarrhea, hence intravenous magnesium sulfate is given.

Allantoin is the end product of purine catabolism in a patient on rasburicase, a recombinant uricase enzyme.
Uric acid is the natural end product of purine catabolism in humans. candidates.value:
The above given clinical findings is suggestive of xeroderma pigmentosum. Defect in the removal of oligonucleotides containing the damaged bases by endonucleases is seen in xeroderma pigmentosum.
Xeroderma Pigmentosum (XP) is a rare autosomal recessive genetic disorder characterized by defective DNA repair which leads to clinical and cellular hypersensitivity to ultraviolet radiation and other carcinogenic agents.
Important clinical features are:
Intense cutaneous photosensitivity, xerosis, poikiloderma, actinic keratosis, acute burning under minimal sun exposure, erythemas, hyperpigmented lentiginous macules, and malignant lesions in sun-exposed areas, including basocellular carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and melanoma.
The final diagnosis of XP can be confirmed by special laboratory tests by examining the DNA damage repair in cells from cultures exposed to ultraviolet radiation. The most common tests are skin biopsy and culture of skin fibroblasts.
There is no cure for XP. Treatment consists of minimizing exposure to sunlight and regular dermatological care, as well as surgery for recurrent tumors excision. Patients should be followed up every 3 months. Genetic counseling is important in a family that has an affected child and is considering having more children.

Housekeeping or constitutive genes are those which are expressed at a constant rate in almost all the cells of the body. These genes are required for the basal cellular function. Examples include genes encoding RNA polymerase, ribosomal protein, rRNA, enzymes for glycolysis, etc.

In contrast, inducible genes are those which are expressed under special circumstances. The expression of these genes increase in response to an activator or inducer, or decrease in response to a repressor.

In bacterial operons, a regulatory gene, like the lac I gene, which is present upstream of a set of structural genes, codes for a repressor protein (a transacting factor). candidates.subject: Biochemistry
candidates.value:
The operon model attempts to explain the coordinated control of gene expression in bacteria.

In bacteria, the structural genes that code for proteins involved in a particular metabolic pathway are often found sequentially grouped on the chromosome. The cis-acting regulatory elements that determine the transcription of these genes are also grouped with the structural genes.

The transcription product of the entire operon is a single polycistronic messenger RNA (mRNA). The structural genes described above are coordinately controlled, that is, turned on or off as a unit. This entire package, of structural and regulatory genes, is referred to as an operon. An example of this is the lac operon in Escherichia coli.

Note: Gene regulation in bacteria is important in order to:
• Enable response to environmental stimuli
• Allow cells to adjust promptly to changes in the growth medium
• Alter biochemical capabilities appropriate for available substrate

candidates.subject: Biochemistry
candidates.value:
In the Lac operon model, lactose binds to the repressor protein and inactivates it, thus activating transcription.

When lactose is present in abundance, a small amount of lactose is converted to allolactose. This compound binds to the repressor protein of the lac operon and creates a conformational change. As a result, the repressor cannot bind to the operator and transcription of the structural genes occurs. This is an example of negative regulation.

This can only occur when glucose is absent. In the absence of glucose, adenylyl cyclase is active. This generates sufficient quantities of cAMP which bind to catabolite activator protein (CAP). The cAMP-CAP trans-acting complex binds to the CAP-binding site, another regulatory region present upstream of the structural genes of the operon. This causes RNA polymerase to more efficiently initiate transcription at the promoter site. This is an example of positive regulation.

candidates.subject: Biochemistry
candidates.value:
Two potential devices that eukaryotic cells use to regulate transcription are as follows: DNA methylation and histone acetylation.

DNA methylation occurs by methyltransferases that use S-adenosyl-methionine as the methyl donor. It silences gene expression.

Histone acetylation decreases the positive charge on histone proteins, thus decreasing the strength of their association with negatively charged DNA. This chromatin remodeling relaxes the nucleosome, allowing transcription factors access to specific regions on the DNA. Thus, histone acetylation improves gene expression.

Note: In both eukaryotes and prokaryotes, gene expression is primarily regulated at the level of transcription.

Methylation does not favour euchromatin formation due to changes cytosine residues at CpG islands in DNA.

The transcriptional regulatory regions of active genes often contain a high frequency of CpG dinucleotides (referred to as CpG islands) and they are normally unmethylated. Therefore, methylation is an epigenetic modification that inactivates DNA, and hinders the formation of euchromatin (transcriptionally active chromatin). Epigenetic changes include alterations of chromatin structure by:

• Modification of histones by acetylation or methylation
• Changes in higher-order chromosome structure

• Acetylation of core histones is associated with chromosomal assembly during DNA replication.
• Phosphorylation of histone H1 is associated with the condensation of chromosomes during the replication cycle.
• ADP-ribosylation of histones is associated with DNA repair.
• Methylation of histones is correlated with activation and repression of gene transcription.
• Acetylation of histones H3 and H4 is associated with the activation or inactivation of gene transcription.
• Monoubiquitylation is associated with gene activation, repression, and heterochromatic gene silencing.

PCR is used for DNA profiling (DNA fingerprinting).
The PCR allows the DNA in a single cell, hair follicle, or spermatozoon to be amplified and
analyzed. Thus, the applications of PCR to forensic medicine are obvious. DNA fingerprinting, or
DNA profiling, is used for forensic analysis of crime scenes and paternity testing (Option D).
Other options:
Option A: Short Tandem Repeat (STR) are short sequences of DNA at scattered locations in the
genome, repeated in tandem (one after the other). E.g., CG-CG-CG-CG-CG. The number of these
repeat units varies from person to person but is unique for any given individual and, therefore,
serves as a molecular fingerprint.
Option B: Single Nucleotide Polymorphism(SNP) refers to variations that involve just one base at
a given locus (Eg., base C replaced by base A), which can occur within exons, introns, intergenic or
coding regions. They are almost always biallelic and are majorly used in the definition of inherited
diseases where the functional deficit is unknown. Each of these variations is present to some
appreciable degree within a population and hence not unique to an individual.

Mechanofeceptors and extéroceptors have the same classification of receptors.
Exteroceptors are concerned with the external environment or receptors which receives external
stimuli. Mechanoreceptors are cutaneous receptors for touch and pressure. Thus
mechanoreceptors can be considered to be exteroceptors.
Nociceptors are pain receptors which detect physical and chemical damage occuring in the tissue.
Interoceptors are concerned with the internal environment.
Chemoreceptors are receptors stimulated by a change in the chemical composition of the
environment in which they are located. These include receptors for taste and smell as well as,
visceral receptors such as those sensitive to changes in the plasma level of O2, pH, and osmolality.
Teleceptors (distance receivers) are concerned with events at a distance, example -
photoreceptors.
Proprioceptors provide information about the position of the body in space at any given instant.

ventrolateral spinothalamic tract) and descending motor (corticospinal tract) pathways, which is
called the Brown-Séquard syndrome.

touch, vibration, and proprioception below the level of the lesion.

‘The loss of the spinothalamic tract leads to contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation
beginning one or two segments below the lesion.
Damage to the corticospinal tract produces weakness and spasticity in certain muscle groups on
the same side of the body.

to prevent tearing of the muscle or avulsion of the tendon from its attachments to the bone.

candidates.subject: Physiology
candidates.value:
The function of the neocerebellum is planning and programming of voluntary movements.
The cerebellum can be divided into:
The Vestibulocerebellum/Archicerebellum: Consists principally of the flocculonodular lobe and adjacent portions of the vermis. It participates in balance, vestibular reflexes, and eye movements.
The Spinocerebellum/Paleocerebellum: Consists of most of the vermis plus the adjacent intermediate zones on both sides of the vermis. It coordinates movements of the limbs. Vermis: Proximal muscles, Intermediate zones: Distal muscles.
The Cerebrocerebellum/neocerebellum: Consists of the large lateral zones of the cerebellar hemispheres. It receives all its input from the cerebral cortex (motor, premotor and somatosensory). It transmits its output back to the brain, functioning in a feedback manner to plan sequential voluntary body and limb movements.

candidates.subject: Physiology
candidates.value:
The amygdala has been called the “window” through which the limbic system sees the place of the person in the world.
The amygdala receives neuronal signals from all portions of the limbic cortex, as well as from the neocortex of the temporal, parietal, and occipital lobes, especially from the auditory and visual association areas.
Components of the limbic system:
• The term limbic lobe, or limbic system, is applied to the part of the brain that consists of a rim of cortical tissue around the hilum of the cerebral hemisphere and a group of associated deep structures—the amygdala, the hippocampus, and the septal nuclei.
• The Papez circuit is a closed neural circuitry that starts and ends in the hippocampus, which forms the basal ganglia. It is also known as the medial limbic circuit. The components of Papez circuit are given by the mnemonic He Man Ate Cat: He-Hippocampus; Man-Mamillary body; Ate-Anterior thalamus; Cat-Cingulate gyrus.

candidates.value:
In the hypothalamus, the suprachiasmatic nucleus functions as the principal pacemaker, or time clock, for circadian rhythms.
The pacemaker receives input from the eyes and many other parts of the nervous system, and these inputs mediate the effects exerted by the external environment (retinohypothalamic tract).
One output of the pacemaker goes to the pineal gland, a gland within the brain that secretes the hormone melatonin. These neural signals cause the pineal gland to secrete melatonin during darkness but not during daylight.

candidates.subject: Physiology
candidates.value:
Functions of the categorical hemisphere are logical, analytical, sequential thinking, and verbal tasks, such as math, language forms, and philosophy.
Human language functions depend more on one cerebral hemisphere than on the other. This hemisphere is concerned with categorization and symbolization and has often been called the dominant hemisphere. However, the other hemisphere is specialized in the area of spatiotemporal relations.
The concept of “cerebral dominance” and a dominant and non-dominant hemisphere has been replaced by one hemisphere for sequential-analytic processes (the categorical hemisphere) and one for visuospatial relations (the representational hemisphere).
The representational cerebral hemisphere excels in nonlanguage skills, especially spatial perception, and artistic and musical talents.

High-frequency stimulation of the midbrain reticular formation (the RAS) produces the EEG
alerting response and arouses a sleeping animal.
The Reticular Activating System (RAS) is a complex polysynaptic pathway arising from the
brainstem reticular formation and hypothalamus with projections to the intralaminar and
reticular nuclei of the thalamus which, in turn, project diffusely and nonspecifically to wide
regions of the cortex including the frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital cortices.
Collaterals funnel into it from the long ascending sensory tracts, the trigeminal, auditory, visual,
and olfactory systems.

The reticular formation plays an important role in determining the level of arousal; thus, it is
called the ascending reticular activating system (ARAS).

candidates.subject: Physiology
candidates.value:
The mechanism of action of surfactant is by breaking the structure of water in alveoli.
When water forms a surface with air, the water molecules on the surface of the alveoli have a
strong attraction for one another. This pulls the molecules together, leading to high surface
tension.
The surfactant is amphipathic in nature (i.e., hydrophobic on one end and hydrophilic on the
other). They align themselves on the alveolar surface, with their hydrophobic portions facing the
alveolar lumen.
The cohesive force between a water molecule and an adjacent pulmonary surfactant molecule is
very low. So, they break up the attracting forces between water molecules lining the alveoli (which
had been responsible for the high surface tension). Thus, they reduce surface tension.

Work done in quiet breathing is 0.5 kg-m/min.
Estimates of the total work of quiet breathing range from 0.3 up to 0.8 kg-m/min.
The work of breathing can be calculated from the pressure-volume curve.

The value rises markedly during exercise, but the energy cost of breathing in normal individuals
represents less than 3% of the total energy expenditure during exercise.
Applied aspect:
In the case of COPD, airway resistance increases (obstruction to outflow). Hence, the patient
should take slow, deep breathing.
In the case of restrictive lung disease, viscous resistance increases. Hence, the patient is advised
rapid, shallow breathing.

candidates.subject: Physiology
candidates.value:
The percentage of cardiac output that bypasses the pulmonary circulation or physiological shunt is 2%. The fraction of mixed venous blood that does not become oxygenated as it moves from the right atrium to the left ventricle is called physiologic shunt.

Causes of physiological shunt:
• Extrapulmonary R→L anatomic shunt (normally ~1% of cardiac output)
• Intrapulmonary “true” shunt
• Flow past unventilated or collapsed alveoli (e.g., due to edema, pneumonia, atelectasis)
• Anatomic arterio-venous pathways: mixing of unoxygenated blood in bronchial veins with oxygenated blood in pulmonary capillaries or vein reduces the final partial pressure of O2 in the arterial blood (PaO2)
• Intrapulmonary regions with low ventilation/perfusion ratio: alveolar ventilation is not zero, but blood is not completely oxygenated (a virtual shunt, not a “true” shunt).

candidates.subject: Physiology
candidates.value:
The diffusing capacity for CO (DLCO) is measured as an index of the diffusing capacity of the lung because its uptake is diffusion-limited.

The diffusing capacity of the lung for a given gas is directly proportional to the surface area of the alveolo-capillary membrane and inversely proportional to its thickness.

DLCO = Amount of CO entering the blood / (Partial pressure of CO in the alveoli − Partial pressure of CO in the blood)

The normal value of DLCO at rest is about 25 mL/min/mm Hg. It increases up to threefold during exercise because of capillary dilation and an increase in the number of active capillaries.

candidates.subject: Physiology
candidates.value:
The partial pressure of water vapor at a normal body temperature of 37°C is 47 mm Hg.

Humidification of air:
• When dry air enters the respiratory system it is humidified, i.e. water molecules are continually escaping from the water surface (tissues) into the gas phase.
• The partial pressure that the water molecules exert to escape through the surface is called the vapor pressure of the water.
• The vapor pressure of water depends entirely on the temperature of the water.
• The greater the temperature, the greater the kinetic activity of the molecules and, therefore, the greater the likelihood that the water molecules will escape from the surface of the water into the gas phase.
• For instance, the water vapor pressure at 0°C is 5 mm Hg, and at 100°C it is 760 mm Hg.
• The most important value to remember is the vapor pressure at body temperature: 47 mm Hg.

Once equilibrium is attained after diffusion, vapour pressure is called partial pressure.

candidates.subject: Physiology
candidates.value:
In healthy individuals, anatomical dead space and physiological dead space are almost equivalent, and can be estimated by body weight.

Dead space is the volume of the airways and lungs that do not participate in gas exchange.

Types:
• Anatomic dead space: volume of the air-occupying conducting zone where no exchange of gases takes place.
• Alveolar/functional dead space: the volume of gas not equilibrating with blood (wasted ventilation).
• Total dead space/physiological dead space = Anatomical + Alveolar dead space.

In healthy individuals:
• Anatomical dead space = 150 mL.
• Alveolar dead space is usually zero (increased in diseased conditions).
• Physiological dead space = Anatomical + Alveolar = 150 + 0 = 150 mL.
• Physiological dead space = Anatomical dead space.
• Radford's formula: anatomical dead space in mL is approximately equal to the body weight in pounds.

Dead space can be measured by:
• Single Breath N2 method (Fowler's method)
• Bohr's equation.

VA/Q = infinity means that there is no exchange of O2 & CO2, which means the volume of the lung equals to dead space and the physiological effort of breathing is wasted.

VA represents the ventilation in alveoli and Q represents the blood flow through the alveolus. The ratio of VA and Q explains the respiratory exchange when there is an imbalance between alveolar ventilation and alveolar blood flow. The ventilation-perfusion ratio is considered normal if there is an equal amount of blood flow & ventilation through the alveolus.

VA/Q ratio is infinity when:
• There is adequate ventilation but no perfusion.
• No exchange of gases (O2 and CO2) through the respiratory membranes of corresponding alveoli.
• The alveolar air equilibrates the humidified inspired air.
• Partial pressures of the O2 and CO2 are 149 mmHg & 0 mm Hg respectively.

Decreased ventilation-perfusion ratio implies decreased oxygenation due to decreased ventilation with respect to perfusion. Hence, PAO2 decreases and PCO2 increases.

A decrease in the ventilation-perfusion ratio (VA/Q) is depicted by moving to the left along the normal ventilation-perfusion line as shown in the figure.

• Zone 1: lowest ventilation compared to Zones 2 and 3, but V >> Q, hence V/Q is high.
• PAO2 is highest.
• PACO2 is lowest.

• Zone 3: highest ventilation compared to Zones 2 and 1, but Q >> V, hence V/Q is low.
• PAO2 is lowest.
• PACO2 is highest.

PACO2 = Alveolar partial pressure of CO2.

candidates.value:
Alveolar gas equation is used to calculate partial pressure of O2 in alveolar air.

PAO2 = PIO2 − (PACO2/R) + correction factor

Where:
• PAO2 = Alveolar PO2 (mm Hg)
• PIO2 = PO2 in inspired air (mm Hg)
• PACO2 = Alveolar PCO2 (mm Hg), which is normally 40 mmHg
• R = Respiratory exchange ratio or respiratory quotient (CO2 production/O2 consumption)
• Correction factor is usually negligible.

Step 1: In the question PO2 in inspired air is not given directly. It has to be calculated:
PIO2 = FIO2 (PB − PH2O)

Where:
• FIO2 = Fraction of inspired O2 (50% or 0.5)
• PB = Barometric pressure (760 mmHg)
• PH2O = Water vapour pressure (47 mmHg)

Substituting:
PIO2 = 0.5 (760 − 47) = 0.5 × 713 = 356.5 mmHg

Step 2:
PAO2 = PIO2 − (PCO2/R) = 356.5 − (40/0.8) = 356.5 − 50 = 306.5 mmHg.

candidates.subject: Physiology
candidates.value:
In emphysema, the destruction of the alveolar walls brings down the diffusion area.

Changes in Emphysema:
• Due to the destruction of the alveolar walls, there is a decrease in surface/diffusion area.
• Cardiac output will be normal.
• Pulmonary artery pressure may be elevated because the destruction of alveoli leads to loss of surrounding capillaries which forces blood into remaining capillaries, which tends to increase pulmonary artery pressure.
• Alveolar PCO2 will tend to increase due to difficulty in expiration.

Diffusion capacity of Lung for CO (DLCO):
• In case of emphysema – Decreased diffusion (DLCO) because of decreased surface area (trypsin destroys respiratory membrane)
• In case of fibrosis or pulmonary edema – Decreased diffusion (DLCO) because of increased thickness of membrane
• In case of anemia – Decreased DLCO
• Polycythemia, pulmonary hemorrhage – Increased DLCO.

candidates.subject: Physiology
candidates.value:
During moderate exercise, there is no change in arterial pO2, arterial pCO2 or arterial pH.

Ventilation increases abruptly at the onset of exercise due to psychic stimuli and afferent impulses from proprioceptors in muscles, tendons, and joints. This is followed by a brief pause and then a gradual increase in ventilation. This gradual increase in ventilation is believed to be due to multiple factors such as an increase in body temperature, increase in plasma K+ level stimulating peripheral chemoreceptors, or the sensitivity of the neurons controlling the response to CO2.

In strenuous exercise, at a certain point, the O2 uptake reaches its maximum levels, beyond which it cannot increase further. This leads to a rise in blood lactate levels. Buffering of lactic acid liberates CO2 which further increases ventilation. The increased production of lactic acid, increase in ventilation and CO2 production are proportional, and alveolar and arterial CO2 changes little to nil. This is called isocapnic buffering.

HDF is the fetal variant of hemoglobin.

The B chains of adult hemoglobin (hemoglobin A) are replaced by y chains in HbF. This

fetus.

• Binding of O2 with hemoglobin tends to displace CO2 from the blood. This effect is important in promoting CO2 transport.
• The combination of O2 with hemoglobin in the lungs causes the hemoglobin to become a stronger acid. This displaces CO2 from the blood.

candidates.subject: Physiology
candidates.chapter: Respiratory Adaptations in Hypoxia, Anemia and with Pressure Changes
candidates.value:
Hypoxic hypoxia is characterized by low partial pressure of O2 in arterial blood (PaO2), while other parameters like partial pressure of CO2 in arterial blood (PaCO2) may remain normal.

Ventilation-Perfusion Imbalance:
• The patchy ventilation-perfusion imbalance is the most common cause of hypoxic hypoxia or hypoxemia.
• If alveoli are not ventilated but perfusion is present - blood passing through that alveoli remains unoxygenated.
• When this unoxygenated blood mixes with blood from normal or overventilated alveoli, there is a right to left shunt created.
• This results in reduced partial pressure of O2 in arterial blood (PaO2) i.e., hypoxemia and consequently hypoxia.

Note:
• Hypoxemia can be defined as a condition where arterial oxygen tension or partial pressure of oxygen (PaO2) is below normal.
• Hypoxia is defined as the reduction of oxygen supply at the tissue level, which is not measured directly by a laboratory value.

Scenario 1:
• Generally, the presence of hypoxemia suggests hypoxia i.e. if there is less oxygen in blood, O2 supply to tissues will also be reduced.
• But, in case of cyanide poisoning, there is hypoxia in the absence of hypoxemia, i.e., arterial O2 content is normal but tissues are not able to utilize it because cyanide interferes with aerobic metabolism in the tissues.

Scenario 2:
• Hypoxia may not be present in patients with hypoxemia if the patient compensates for a low PaO2 by increasing oxygen delivery. This is typically achieved by increasing cardiac output (by raising the heart rate) or decreasing tissue oxygen consumption.
• Nevertheless, hypoxemia is definitely the most common cause of tissue hypoxia, and the correct diagnosis should be made because it is readily treatable.

candidates.subject: Physiology
candidates.chapter: Respiratory Adaptations in Hypoxia, Anemia and with Pressure Changes
candidates.value:
In the case of anemic hypoxia, O2 content is low but dissolved O2 is within normal limits, so it does not stimulate peripheral chemoreceptors.

Peripheral chemoreceptors located in the carotid and aortic arteries sense changes in PO2 (<60 mm Hg), pH, and PCO2 and they respond to changes in dissolved O2 (PaO2).

Histotoxic hypoxia will lead to metabolic acidosis that will lead to an increase in H+ concentration, which in turn will stimulate the peripheral chemoreceptors.

Hemorrhage that produces hypotension leads to chemoreceptor stimulation due to decreased blood flow to the chemoreceptors and consequent stagnant anoxia of these organs.

Note: In case of stagnant hypoxia, chemoreceptors can be stimulated if the resultant decreased oxygen delivery causes a significant drop in local tissue oxygen levels, which eventually can lower the PaO2 detectable by chemoreceptors. Therefore, they may not be significantly stimulated unless the reduction in oxygen levels is severe. Therefore, anaemic hypoxia is a better answer.

candidates.value:
In stagnant hypoxia, blood flow is very low; so, more oxygen is extracted causing an increase in reduced hemoglobin → cyanosis.

Cyanosis - Cyanosis is the dusky bluish discoloration of the tissues occurring when the reduced hemoglobin concentration is more than 5 g/dL.

Its occurrence depends upon:
• The total amount of hemoglobin in the blood
• Degree of hemoglobin unsaturation
• The state of capillary circulation

Option a: In the case of anemia, the total hemoglobin content is low, so enough reduced hemoglobin cannot be formed.

Option b: In histotoxic hypoxia, the amount of reduced hemoglobin formed is very less because the defect is in the tissue O2.

Option c: In CO poisoning, there is the formation of carboxyhemoglobin, which is red in color and obscures the color of reduced hemoglobin.

candidates.subject: Physiology
candidates.chapter: Respiratory Adaptations in Hypoxia, Anemia and with Pressure Changes
candidates.value:
Administration of oxygen has maximum benefit in hypoxic hypoxia.

Hypoxic hypoxia refers to a condition in which there is low atmospheric PO2, leading to low arterial PO2. Hence, supplemental O2 can be very beneficial when the cause of hypoxia is due to limited oxygen availability.

Administration of oxygen-rich gas has limited value in anemic, histotoxic, and stagnant hypoxia because:

Anemic hypoxia - Oxygen delivery is not beneficial because despite increasing the exogenous oxygen delivery, an anemic person will not have the capacity to carry more oxygen due to the hemoglobin/red blood cell deficit in anemia.

Histotoxic hypoxia - The most common example is cyanide poisoning. Cyanide inhibits important enzymes in the oxidative phosphorylation process, which is essential to the survival of our cells. Additional oxygen supplementation will not be able to overcome this inhibition, and so it will have limited benefit. Hyperbaric oxygen may be helpful to some extent.

Stagnant hypoxia - Stagnant hypoxia refers to ischemic hypoxia that results from inadequate circulation due to conditions such as heart failure and hypoxia in the setting of shock. In such conditions, administering intravenous fluids can improve the patient's condition because it is the circulation that is affected. If the shock is prolonged it can result in acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), which can be treated with positive pressure ventilation and not simply by increasing oxygen administration.

candidates.chapter: Respiratory Adaptations in Hypoxia, Anemia and with Pressure Changes
candidates.value:
With O2 therapy, increasing the inspired PO2 will result in an increased amount of dissolved O2. At high altitudes, there is low barometric pressure and so less PO2, hence, supplemental O2 will help.

Option A: With anemia, the hemoglobin is fully saturated and O2 will have minimal effect. Treatment of anemia is more beneficial than providing oxygen to an anemic patient.

Option B: With COPD there is CO2 retention due to difficulty in the expiration, and there will be a decreased PO2. So, there is a change in the regulation of respiration (drive for ventilation) from being under CO2 control to being driven by the decrease in O2. Giving supplemental O2 to such a person will increase arterial PO2, thus decrease the stimulus to breathe, resulting in patient stopping breathing.

Option C: Cyanide poisoning results in decreased O2 utilization by the tissues, and so additional O2 would be of no benefit.

candidates.value:
Oxygen therapy is not beneficial in central respiratory depression.

High dose oxygen reduces the output of peripheral chemoreceptors. So, if given to patients who already have central respiratory depression, it will indirectly reduce the hypoxic drive to breathe even further, leading to a reduction in respiratory frequency and minute ventilation.

Note: In acute severe asthma, a high concentration of oxygen should be given by face mask to achieve an oxygen saturation of 94-96%.

candidates.value:
Curve C corresponds to blood from an adult (dark blue line) and blood from a fetus (light blue line). The fetal oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve is shifted to the left relative to the adult curve.

The fetal hemoglobin (Hb F) has a greater affinity for O2 than adult hemoglobin (Hb A). This facilitates the movement of O2 from the mother to fetus. The cause of this greater affinity is the poor binding of 2,3-DPG by γ polypeptide chains that replace β chains in Hb F. The fetal oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve is thus shifted to the left relative to the adult curve. Typically, fetal arterial PO2 is low, hence leftward shift enhances placental uptake of O2.

candidates.chapter: Respiratory Adaptations in Hypoxia, Anemia and with Pressure Changes
candidates.value:
The right shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin curve allows more oxygen to be released to the muscle at a given PO2 in the blood. The oxygen dissociation curve shifts to the right when factors like:
• Increased temperature resulting from heat generated by the exercising muscle
• Higher carbon dioxide level released from the muscle tissue
• Elevated 2,3-Bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG)
• Increased hydrogen ions concentration in the muscle capillary blood

Above factors decrease hemoglobin's oxygen affinity. This shift promotes easier oxygen release to muscles and other tissues.

Note: Despite the rightward shift, the maximum hemoglobin oxygen saturation at high oxygen levels remains unchanged. The plateau on the curve represents the maximal saturation achievable under optimal conditions, ensuring hemoglobin can still be fully saturated with oxygen.

candidates.subject: Physiology
candidates.chapter: Respiratory Adaptations in Hypoxia, Anemia and with Pressure Changes
candidates.value:
Decompression sickness is seen in pilots, mountaineers, and divers.

Decompression sickness (DCS) or diver's disease, the bends, or Caisson disease is the name given to a variety of symptoms experienced by a person exposed to a reduction in the pressure surrounding their body.

It can be seen in:
• Divers ascending rapidly from deep-sea (high pressure) to the surface of the earth (low pressure)
• Pilots traveling in unpressurized aircraft or mountaineers, rapidly ascending from the surface of the earth (high-pressure zone) to a high altitude (low-pressure zone)

Under high-pressure, gases get compressed and their solubility increases. When a person is in a high-pressure zone like the deep sea for a long time, an increased amount of nitrogen gets dissolved in his or her body. If the person suddenly comes back to an area of atmospheric pressure or a low-pressure zone, the gases escape from a dissolved state and form bubbles. These bubbles are almost entirely made of nitrogen. The bubbles can plug many small blood vessels in different tissues.

candidates.subject: Physiology
candidates.chapter: Respiratory Adaptations in Hypoxia, Anemia and with Pressure Changes
candidates.value:
Nitrogen narcosis is due to increased solubility of nitrogen in the nerve cell.

Concept:
• Below the sea level, atmospheric pressure increases at the rate of 1 atm for every 33 feet depth.
• According to Boyle's law, as pressure increases, volume decreases. Hence lungs tend to collapse. To prevent this and to keep lung expanded, gas is delivered at high pressure to the lungs.
• According to Dalton's law, nitrogen contributes the maximum to barometric pressure and hence the amount of nitrogen entering alveoli increases.
• Henry's law: As the partial pressure of nitrogen in alveoli increases, its concentration in blood also increases (dissolved form). Nitrogen is 5 times more soluble in fat compared to water.
• As a result, nitrogen dissolves in the fatty substances in neuronal membranes, and because of its physical effect on altering ionic conductance through the membranes, it reduces neuronal excitability and produces the narcotic effect.

candidates.subject: Physiology
candidates.chapter: Respiratory Adaptations in Hypoxia, Anemia and with Pressure Changes
candidates.value:
A shift of Oxygen Haemoglobin Dissociation Curve (OHDC) to the right is seen in acclimatization.

On ascension to higher altitudes over a period of days rather than a period of hours, the ability to breathe much more deeply and withstand lower atmospheric O2 concentrations is improved. This phenomenon is called acclimatization.

Variation of pH in Acclimatization:

Immediate exposure to low PO2 stimulates the arterial chemoreceptors. This increases alveolar ventilation. This immediate increase in pulmonary ventilation upon rising to a high altitude blows off large quantities of CO2, reducing the PCO2 and increases the pH of the body fluids.

These changes inhibit the brain stem respiratory center and thereby oppose the effect of low PO2 to stimulate respiration through the peripheral arterial chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies.

There is a reduction of bicarbonate ion concentration in the cerebrospinal fluid, as well as in the brain tissues. This reduction, in turn, decreases the pH in the fluids surrounding the chemosensitive neurons of the respiratory center, thus increasing the respiratory stimulatory activity of the center. An important mechanism for the gradual decrease in bicarbonate concentration is compensation by the kidneys for the respiratory alkalosis. Gradually, the metabolic compensation of the kidney will shift the pH towards normal.

candidates.chapter: Respiratory Adaptations in Hypoxia, Anemia and with Pressure Changes
candidates.value:
The symptoms of headache and breathlessness following rapid ascent indicate acute mountain/altitude sickness and IV digoxin is not used to treat this condition.

On ascent to high altitudes, the low partial pressure of oxygen leads to hypoxia and systemic arteriolar dilatation. Consequently, the capillary pressure rises with increased transudation of fluid into the brain tissue and the following symptoms are seen:
• Headache
• Irritation
• Insomnia
• Breathlessness
• Nausea and vomiting

Treatment involves administration of oxygen, descent to a lower altitude and administration of acetazolamide. Acetazolamide counteracts hypoxia by stimulating respiration and also reduces the formation of cerebrospinal fluid, thereby reducing intracranial tension.

Portable hyperbaric chambers are increasingly being used in the treatment of high-altitude illnesses when rapid descent is not possible. These chambers are available in armed forces hospitals in high altitude areas.

The factor favoring filtration at the arterial end of the capillary bed is the increase in hydrostatic pressure of the capillary.

• πc = capillary colloidal osmotic pressure
• πi = interstitial colloidal osmotic pressure

Glomerular filtration rate = k × NFP

• k = capillary filtration coefficient
• NFP = Net filtration pressure

candidates.value:
Factor 2 would have decreased gamma carboxyglutamate residue in a patient on warfarin therapy.

Activation of coagulation factors II, VII, IX, X is done by carboxylation of their glutamate residues. This is done by the enzyme γ-glutamyl carboxylase with the reduced form of vitamin K as a co-factor.

This reduced form of vitamin K needs to be constantly recycled back from its oxidized form for the reaction to continue. This recycling is done by the enzyme vitamin K epoxide reductase. This enzyme is inhibited by warfarin.

Hence, warfarin indirectly inhibits the γ-carboxylation of vitamin K dependent clotting factors — Factors II, VII, IX, X — by directly inhibiting vitamin K epoxide reductase. Thus leading to decreased gamma carboxyglutamate residue in these factors.

Inferior vena cava has the highest oxygen concentration in fetal circulation.

The blood gets oxygenated in the placenta and this passes to the umbilical vein. From the
umbilical vein, 50% of the blood enters the hepatic circulation and 50% bypasses the liver to enter
the inferior vena cava. From here, the blood enters the heart via the right atrium. The right atrium
also receives deoxygenated blood from the superior vena cava. This mixed blood is distributed to
the body via aorta. e@

Therefore, inferior vena cava has the highest concentration of oxygen in the fetal Girculation.

The most powerful activator of the sympathetic vasomotor system is CNS ischemic response.

CNS ischemic response:

When blood flow to the vasomotor center in lower brainstem (medulla) is severely decreased, the
local concentration of CO2 increases greatly and has a potent effect in stimulating the sympathetic
vasomotor nervous control areas in the brain’s medulla. Blood pressure may increase till 250
mmHg. The strong activation may cause some peripheral vessels to occlude.

It doesnt activate till arterial pressure drops to 60mmHg or less, hence it is principally a
emergency mechanism.

Note: Baroreceptors are the most common activators, but not the most powerful.

candidates.value:
Blood flow per minute in the pulmonary circulation is equal to flow through the systemic
circulation so as to provide continuous blood supply to the body.

If the flow rate is slower in the pulmonary circulation than systemic, then the left ventricle would
soon empty completely. If the flow rate is faster in the pulmonary circulation then the left
ventricle would be soon overloaded.

Please note that because some blood flows into the bronchial arteries, the actual flow through the
pulmonary circulation is slightly lesser than the flow through the systemic circulation. However,
this question aims to state that the blood flow through both pulmonary and systemic circulation is
largely equal.

vessels.

The initiating cause of this blockage is sluggish blood flow in the microvessels. Tissue metabolites
plus other deterioration products from the ischemic tissues causes minute clots in these vessels.
Thus the microvasculature gets blocked by the sludged blood.

In progressive hemorrhagic shock, there is increased lysosomal activity, decreased active
transport of sodium and tissue acidosis.

The "flow" phase (not "ebb") leads to activation of the innate immune system and induction of the
hepatic acute-phase response.
Cuthbertson's ebb and flow response to trauma:

The "ebb" phase lasts for a brief duration and is associated with a decline in body temperature and
oxygen consumption, aimed at reducing post traumatic energy depletion.

The "flow" phase occurs after resuscitation from a state of shock, which leads to an increased
metabolic turnover, activation of the innate immune system and induction of the hepatic
acute-phase response. This hypercatabolic condition leads to a significantly increased oxygen
consumption and energy expenditure.

candidates.subject: Physiology
candidates.value:
Phase 0 of pacemaker potential is initiated by opening of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels.
The pacemaker potential consists of:
• Phase 0 - This is upstroke seen due to the opening of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels. This causes an influx of calcium leading to the upstroke.
• Phase 3 - This is followed by inactivation of the calcium channels and simultaneous activation of K+ channels. This leads to efflux of K+ bringing about repolarization.
• Phase 4 - As the K+ efflux declines, a channel permeable to both Na+ and K+ opens leading to an influx of both Na+ and K+. This is the If channel. This is responsible for slow spontaneous diastolic depolarization. This accounts for the automaticity of SA and AV node.
The slope of Phase 4 in the SA node determines the heart rate.
Note: Fast voltage-gated Na+ channels seen in myocyte potential are permanently inactivated because of the less negative resting potential of the pacemaker cells.

The carotid sinus baroreceptor is most sensitive to pulse pressure. They fire more rapidly to a constantly changing pressure than a stationary one.

Baroreceptors

• Stretch receptors located in the heart and adventitia of the blood vessels
• Types based on location
• Carotid sinus and aortic arch receptors (high-pressure regions)
• Cardiopulmonary receptors (low-pressure regions)
• Afferents
• Carotid sinus - a branch of Glossopharyngeal nerve (IX CN) - the carotid sinus nerve (sinus nerve of Hering)
• Aortic arch receptor - a branch of the Vagus nerve (X CN) - aortic depressor nerve
• Center for Reflex
• Medulla (Nucleus Tractus solitarius)
• Efferents
• Sympathetic and parasympathetic neurons to heart and vasculature
• Most sensitive to pulsatile pressure: They work to maintain BP in the range of mean BP, but it is the changes in the pressure they are the most sensitive to.
• The threshold for excitation: 50 mmHg
• Maximal activity: 180 mmHg
• Responses when one carotid sinus is isolated and perfused and the other baroreceptors are denervated
• Perfusion pressure <30 mm Hg: no response
• 70-110 mm Hg: the linear relationship between perfusion pressure and the fall in systemic BP and HR
• >150 mm Hg: no further increase in response to the degree of inhibition of the sympathetic nerve is maximal.

Discharge from Baroreceptors cause inhibition of Rostral ventrolateral medulla.

The baroreceptors are stimulated by distension of the structures in which they are located. Their afferent fibers pass via the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves to the medulla. candidates.subject: Physiology
candidates.value:
Reflex responsible for tachycardia during right atrial distension is Bainbridge Reflex.

The stretch receptors of the atria that elicit the Bainbridge reflex transmit their afferent signals through the vagus nerves to the medulla of the brain. Then efferent signals are transmitted back through vagal and sympathetic nerves to increase heart rate and strength of heart contraction. Thus, this reflex helps prevent damming of blood in the veins, atria, and pulmonary circulation.

Other options:

Option A: Bezold-Jarisch Reflex: Activation of chemosensitive vagal C fibers in the cardiopulmonary region causes profound bradycardia, hypotension and a brief period of apnoea followed by rapid shallow breathing.

Option C: Cushing Reflex: When intracranial pressure is increased, the blood supply to Rostral Ventro-Lateral Medulla (RVLM) neurons is compromised. The local hypoxia and hypercapnia cause an increase in discharge from the neurons, producing hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular respiration.

Option D: J Reflex: The stimulation of the J-receptors (C receptors/juxta-pulmonary capillary receptors) causes apnea followed by rapid breathing, bradycardia, and hypotension.

candidates.subject: Physiology
candidates.value:
The reflex responsible for elevated blood pressure (BP) in head injury patients is the Cushing reflex.

When intracranial pressure is increased, the blood supply to rostral ventrolateral neurons is compromised, and the local hypoxia and hypercapnia increase the discharge of the central chemoreceptors. The resultant rise in systemic arterial pressure (Cushing reflex) tends to restore the blood flow to the medulla.

Cushing reflex causes a triad of symptoms:

• Reflex bradycardia (via arterial baroreceptors)
• Hypertension (with widened pulse pressure)
• Irregular respiration (bradypnea)

candidates.subject: Physiology

Glucose is absorbed in the intestine by secondary active transport.

On the basolateral side, there is active transport of sodium ions out of the cell into the interstitial fluid. This depletes sodium inside the cell. Because of this Na+ concentration difference, more Na+ binds to the SGLT on the luminal side. This increases the affinity of SGLT for glucose and glucose binds to it.

Then, both the Na+ and glucose are transported together to the interior of the cell. Thus, glucose is absorbed in the intestine by secondary active transport. The energy for glucose transport is provided indirectly, by the active transport of Na+ out of the cell. The glucose moves out of the cell into the blood across the basolateral membrane by facilitated diffusion mediated via GLUT.

Interstitial cells of Cajal are the pacemaker cells of the GIT that initiate the basic electrical rhythm (BER). These are stellate mesenchymal pacemaker cells with smooth muscle-like features.

candidates.subject: Physiology
candidates.value:
Among the given options, the least frequency of slow waves is seen in the stomach (4/min).

The Basal electrical rhythm (BER), also called slow-wave, is a rhythmic fluctuation of membrane potential in the gastrointestinal smooth muscle. It is initiated by the interstitial cells of Cajal. The membrane potential fluctuates between -65 mV and -45 mV.

The BER is seen in all sites of gastrointestinal smooth muscle except in the esophagus and proximal stomach.

The rate of BER in various sites is as follows:
• Stomach: 4/min
• Duodenum: 12/min
• Distal ileum: 8/min
• Cecum: 2/min
• Sigmoid colon: 6/min

The BER does not cause contraction of the smooth muscle. However, when the BER is superimposed by the spike potentials, it increases muscle tension.

Acetylcholine causes an increase in the number of spike potentials and muscle tension. Epinephrine causes a decrease in the number of spike potentials and muscle tension.

Muscle contraction can occur only when the motor stimulus is provided during the depolarisation part of the BER.

Thus, BER does not cause muscle contraction by itself, but controls the rate and organization sites of the muscle contractions, as in coordination of the peristaltic activity and setting the rhythm of segmentation.

candidates.subject: Physiology
candidates.value:
Among the given options, the frequency of 'slow waves' is maximum in the ileum (8/min).

Normal intestinal motility is determined by two patterns of electrical activity - slow waves and spike potentials.

Slow waves, also known as basic electrical rhythm, are partial depolarizations of smooth muscle cells, spreading along the GIT. They originate from the interstitial cells of Cajal. The smooth muscles are in a hyperpolarized state, having a resting membrane potential of -50 to -60 mV.

These waves are not action potentials themselves and they do not cause any contractions. Slow waves raise the membrane potential by 5-15 mV, bringing it closer to the threshold enabling spike potential (true action potential) to occur. Therefore, they set the basic rhythm of GIT.

Chyme is propelled forward in the intestine by the peristaltic movement.

Chyme is a thick semifluid mass of partially digested food and digestive secretions that is expelled by the stomach into the duodenum.

Peristalsis is a propulsive movement, which consists of a segment of contraction behind and relaxation in front.

Migrating motor complexes (MMC) are the peristaltic motor patterns that occur during fasting. They migrate from the stomach to the distal ileum.

Haustrations are the characteristic saclike segments seen in the large intestine.

candidates.value:
Gastric emptying is mainly regulated by enteric reflexes.

Regulation of gastric emptying is mainly by the inhibitory feedback signals from the duodenum that includes enterogastric reflex and hormonal feedback by cholecystokinin.

Enterogastric reflex: When food enters the duodenum, multiple nervous reflexes are initiated from the duodenal wall. They strongly inhibit the pyloric pump propulsive contractions and increase the tone of the pyloric sphincter.

These reflexes are mediated by three routes:
• Directly from the duodenum to the stomach through the enteric nervous system in the gut wall (major role)
• Through inhibitory sympathetic nerve fibers to the stomach (minor role)
• Vagus nerves to the brain stem where they inhibit the normal excitatory signals transmitted to the stomach (minor role)

Hormonal feedback: Cholecystokinin is released from the mucosa of the jejunum in response to fatty substances in the chyme. This hormone acts as an inhibitor to block increased stomach motility caused by gastrin.

Enterogastric reflex: When food enters the duodenum, multiple nervous reflexes are initiated from the duodenal wall. They strongly inhibit the pyloric pump propulsive contractions and increase the tone of the pyloric sphincter.
These reflexes are mediated by three routes:
• Directly from the duodenum to the stomach through the enteric nervous system in the gut wall (major role)
• Through inhibitory sympathetic nerve fibers to the stomach (minor role)
• Vagus nerves to the brain stem where they inhibit the normal excitatory signals transmitted to the stomach (minor role)

Hormonal feedback: Cholecystokinin is released from the mucosa of the jejunum in response to fatty substances in the chyme. This hormone acts as an inhibitor to block increased stomach motility caused by gastrin.

candidates.subject: Physiology
candidates.value:
In the enterogastric reflex, gastric emptying is delayed when acidic content enters the duodenum.

When the food enters the duodenum, multiple reflexes are initiated from the duodenal wall which pass back to the stomach. These reflexes slow or stop the stomach emptying if the volume of the chyme in the duodenum becomes too much. These reflexes are called enterogastric reflexes.

This reflex can be triggered due to the following reasons:
• Presence of irritants and acids in duodenal chyme (most sensitive factor)
• Distension of duodenum due to the presence of an excessive volume of chyme
• Rapid entry of hypertonic or hypotonic fluids into the duodenum
• Presence of breakdown products of protein digestion and sometimes fat

candidates.subject: Physiology
candidates.value:
Enterogastric inhibitory reflexes are stimulated by acidic contents, not alkaline.

The duodenal factors that can initiate enterogastric inhibitory reflexes (enterogastric reflexes) are:
• Distention of the duodenum
• Presence of any irritation of the duodenal mucosa
• Acidity of the duodenal chyme
• Osmolality of the chyme: either hypotonic or hypertonic fluid initiate enterogastric inhibitory reflexes. Thus, the flow of non-isotonic fluids into the small intestine is regulated. This prevents rapid changes in electrolyte concentrations in the extracellular fluid during the absorption of the intestinal contents.
• Presence of certain breakdown products in the chyme, especially proteins and to a lesser extent, of fats

candidates.subject: Physiology
candidates.value:
Migrating motor complex (MMC) migrates from the stomach to the distal ileum at a rate of about 5 cm/min and also occurs at intervals of approximately 100 minutes.

MMC is a type of gastrointestinal motility that occurs during fasting between periods of digestion. It is initiated by motilin. It helps to clear the stomach and small intestine of luminal contents in preparation for the next meal. Gastric secretion, bile flow, and pancreatic secretion increase during each MMC.

After ingestion of a meal, secretion of motilin is suppressed and the MMC is abolished.

Each cycle of MMC has 3 phases:
• Phase I - quiescent period
• Phase II - period of irregular electrical & mechanical activity
• Phase III - ends with bursts of regular activity

Note: Disorders of MMC have been associated with gastroparesis, intestinal pseudo-obstruction, and small intestinal bacterial overgrowth.

candidates.subject: Physiology
candidates.value:
From the duodenum, the migrating motor complex (MMC) moves distally at 5-10 cm/min, reaching the terminal ileum after 1.5 hours.

In the fasting state, there is a period of quiescence in the small bowel, lasting for approximately 40 minutes (phase I). This is followed by a series of waves, also lasting for about 40 minutes, propagating from the fundus of the stomach in a caudal direction at a rate of about 3 per minute (phase II).

Duodenal slow waves are generated in the duodenum at a rate of about 10 per minute, which carry down the small bowel.

The amplitude of these contractions increases to a maximum in phase III, which lasts for about 10 minutes. This 90-minute cycle of activity is then repeated.

candidates.subject: Physiology
candidates.value:
Secretin inhibits small intestinal motility.

Factors that increase the peristaltic activity of the small intestine:
• Hormonal - gastrin, CCK, insulin, motilin, and serotonin
• Neural - duodenal distension by chyme, gastroenteric reflexes, gastroileal reflexes, parasympathetic (ACh) stimulation

Factors that decrease the peristaltic activity of the small intestine:
• Hormonal - secretin and glucagon
• Neural - sympathetic stimulation

Gastroileal reflex: On reaching the ileocecal valve, the chyme is sometimes blocked for several hours until the person eats another meal. At that time, a gastroileal reflex intensifies peristalsis in the ileum and forces the remaining chyme through the ileocecal valve into the cecum of the large intestine.

candidates.value:
Efferent arteriolar constriction increases oncotic pressure in glomerular capillaries.
Efferent arteriolar constriction has a biphasic response on GFR depending on the severity of
resistance.

Moderate efferent arteriolar constriction causes increased glomerular hydrostatic pressure and
slightly increased GFR.
However, in cases of severe efferent arteriolar constriction (more than threefold increase in
efferent arteriolar resistance), the renal blood flow is significantly reduced. This results in
increased plasma protein concentration, thereby increasing the glomerular colloid oncotic
pressure. As the increase in colloid oncotic pressure exceeds the increase in hydrostatic pressure,
the net force for filtration decreases, resulting in decreased GFR.

candidates.value: Normal anion gap is mostly due to unmeasured proteins. Normally in plasma, concentrations of anions and cations are equal to maintain electrical neutrality, so no real “anion gap” exists; it is a diagnostic concept. Routinely measured ions are Na+, Cl- and HCO3-. The anion gap is the difference between unmeasured anions and unmeasured cations. Plasma anion gap = [Na+] - [Cl-] - [HCO3-]. The unmeasured cations include calcium, magnesium and potassium. The unmeasured anions include albumin, phosphate, sulphate and organic anions. This is primarily used in measurement of different causes of metabolic acidosis.

The secretion of prolactin is increased after the sectioning of the pituitary stalk.
Prolactin is unique among the pituitary hormones because the predominant central control mechanism is inhibitory, i.e., dopamine inhibits prolactin secretion. Hence, sectioning of the pituitary stalk (Ex: In head trauma or compressive skull lesions) prevents this inhibition and leads to increased secretion of prolactin.

candidates.subject: Physiology
candidates.value:
Iodide trapping (iodide uptake) is not catalyzed by thyroid peroxidase. Oxidation, organification, and coupling are catalyzed by it.
Steps in synthesis and secretion of thyroid hormone:
• Iodide uptake: The basolateral sodium-iodide symporter (NIS) actively takes up I− (iodide) from the circulation into the follicular cells. It is then transported into the colloid through a pendrin (chloride-iodide) transporter.
• Thyroglobulin synthesis: Thyroglobulin (Tg), is a large glycoprotein rich in tyrosine residues. It is synthesized by follicular cells.
• Iodination of thyroglobulin: This is regulated by the thyroid peroxidase (TPO) enzyme. TPO has three functions:
  • Oxidation: TPO oxidizes I− to I2 (iodine) in the presence of H2O2
  • Organification: TPO links tyrosine residues of thyroglobulin with iodine (I2) to form monoiodotyrosine (MIT), diiodotyrosine (DIT)
  • Coupling reactions: TPO combines iodinated tyrosine residues to make MIT + DIT = T3 (triiodothyronine), DIT + DIT = T4 (tetraiodothyronine)
• Storage: Thyroid hormones are bound to thyroglobulin and stored in the follicular lumen as colloids. The colloid has hormone reserves for 2-3 months.
• Release: Iodinated thyroglobulin is taken up by the thyroid follicles via endocytosis and fuses with lysosomes. It is cleaved by lysosomal proteolytic enzymes into MIT, DIT, T3, and T4. T4 (80%) and T3 (20%) are released into the blood.
• Peripheral T3 conversion: T4 undergoes deiodination in extrathyroidal tissue to form T3, which is the active form of the hormone.

Glucose-mediated insulin release occurs through the closure of ATP sensitive K+ channels. Therefore the new drug being initiated is most probably a sulfonylurea which acts via a similar mechanism.
Increased blood glucose concentration is the primary controller of insulin secretion. Inside the beta cells, glucose is converted to glucose-6-phosphate, and later ATP is generated. This ATP closes ATP sensitive potassium channels, leading to a rise in K+ and depolarization. This in turn causes the opening of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels and influx of Ca2+. This ultimately leads to the secretion of insulin via exocytosis.
Diazoxide keeps the ATP sensitive K+ channels open and prevents depolarization, resulting in a decreased insulin release. It is used in patients with insulinoma.
Sulfonylureas cause closure of the ATP sensitive K+ channels, leading to increased insulin secretion. It is used in patients with diabetes mellitus.

An insulin receptor has 4 parts. It is a tetramer made up of two α and two β subunits.

candidates.subject: Physiology
candidates.value:
Insulin inhibits glucose-6-phosphatase.
Insulin promotes liver uptake, storage, and the use of glucose. After a meal, insulin causes glucose to be rapidly stored in the liver in the form of glycogen. This occurs by:

• Enhanced uptake of glucose by the liver cells by increasing the activity of the enzyme glucokinase which causes phosphorylation of glucose after it enters the liver cells. Once phosphorylated, the glucose is temporarily trapped inside the liver cells because phosphorylated glucose cannot diffuse back through the cell membrane.
• Increased activity of enzymes that promote glycogen synthesis, like glycogen synthase.
When insulin levels drop (Example: fasting), glucose phosphatase gets activated. This causes phosphate to get detached from glucose phosphate, allowing free glucose from the liver cells to re-enter circulation.

candidates.subject: Physiology
candidates.value:
Diazoxide acts by opening ATP sensitive K+ channels and causing a decrease in insulin secretion.
Glucose enters beta cells of the pancreas via GLUT-2 receptors. Once inside, it is phosphorylated by glucokinase (rate-limiting step) to glucose-6-phosphate which is oxidized to form adenosine triphosphate (ATP). This ATP causes closure of ATP-sensitive potassium channels and hence depolarization. This leads to opening voltage-gated calcium channels and Ca2+ influx. This stimulates fusion of the insulin-containing vesicles with the cell membrane and secretion of insulin into the extracellular fluid by exocytosis.
Diazoxide keeps the ATP sensitive K+ channels open and prevents depolarization and subsequent insulin release.
Sulfonylureas cause closure of the ATP sensitive K+ channels, leading to increased insulin secretion.

Cortisol suppresses the proliferation of T-lymphocytes and decreases the number of T-lymphocytes.

Actions of Cortisol:
Metabolic effects:
• Effect on carbohydrates: Exerts an anti-insulin effect, leading to hyperglycemia.
• Increases gluconeogenesis.
• Increases glycogen synthesis.
• Decreases utilization of glucose in peripheral tissues.
• Effect on fat and appetite: promotes mobilization of fatty acids from adipose tissue in acute states. This mobilization increases the concentration of free fatty acids in the plasma, which also increases their utilization for energy, causing lipolysis. However, in chronic states cortisol increases appetite and food intake by inducing the synthesis of neuropeptide-Y which leads to an apparent lipogenic effect seen as buffalo humping and central obesity.
• Effect on protein: Exerts a catabolic effect and causes proteolysis.
• Effect on water and electrolytes: Sodium water retention and diuresis.

Anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects:
• Induce the synthesis of lipocortin, an inhibitor of phospholipase A2.
• Inhibit the release of histamine and serotonin.
• Inhibit the production of IL-2 and T lymphocytes, and depress cellular immunity.

Maintenance of vascular responsiveness to catecholamines:
• Cortisol up-regulates α1 receptors on arterioles, increasing their sensitivity to the vasoconstrictor effect of norepinephrine.

Ionic calcium is the active form that is important for most functions of calcium in the body, including the effect of calcium on the heart, the nervous system, and bone formation.

Most of the calcium (99%) is stored in the bones. Only about 0.1 percent of the total body calcium is in the extracellular fluid and 1 percent is in the cells and its organelles.

From the 0.1% Ca²⁺ in the plasma, the distribution of calcium is as follows:
• About 41% is combined with the plasma proteins (non-diffusible through the capillary membrane).
• About 9% is combined with anionic substances of the plasma and interstitial fluids like citrate and phosphate in such a manner that it is not ionized (diffusible through the capillary membrane).
• The remaining 50% of the calcium in the plasma is both diffusible through the capillary membrane and ionized.

candidates.value:
Osteoclasts play a key role in bone resorption.

The cells responsible for bone formation are osteoblasts and the cells responsible for bone resorption are osteoclasts.

Osteoblasts are modified fibroblasts. Osteoclasts are the members of the monocyte family.

Osteoclasts erode and absorb the previously formed bone:
• They become attached to the bone via integrins forming a sealing zone where the bone resorption takes place.
• Proton pumps (H⁺-ATPases) then move from the endosomes of the osteoclasts into the cell membrane as opposed to the sealing zone and acidify the area into pH 4.0.
• The acidic pH dissolves hydroxyapatite and the acid proteases secreted by the cell break down collagen.

candidates.subject: Physiology
candidates.value:
Osteoclast cells do not have PTH receptors. PTH stimulates osteoclast activity and bone resorption by an indirect mechanism.

PTH has receptors on the osteoblasts in the bone. When PTH binds to these receptors, osteoblasts release cytokines like RANK-ligand and M-CSF. These cytokines allow the differentiation of macrophages to osteoclasts.

Osteoclasts, in turn, cut the collagen in the bone, which is bound to calcium. This causes the release of calcium, phosphorus, and collagen breakdown products in the blood.

Osteoblasts produce osteoprotegerin (OPG), or osteoclastogenesis inhibitory factor, a cytokine that inhibits bone resorption by preventing interaction of RANKL with its receptor. PTH decreases the production of osteoprotegerin (OPG).

Glucocorticoids promote osteoclast activity and increase bone resorption by increasing RANKL production and decreasing the formation of OPG. On the other hand, the hormone estrogen stimulates OPG production.

Calcitonin has calcium-lowering effects and may cause hypocalcemia. It does so by inhibiting bone resorption (direct effect).

Calcitonin is synthesized and secreted by parafollicular (clear) cells of the thyroid. Actions of calcitonin are as follows:
• Inhibits osteoclasts, thereby decreasing bone resorption (direct effect).
• Increases renal calcium excretion.
• Decreases calcium absorption by the kidneys and intestines.

Under normal conditions calcitonin is more important in young individuals (compared to adults), and may play a role in skeletal development.

In addition, it may protect the bones of the mother from excess calcium loss during pregnancy. Bone formation in the infant and lactation are major drains on Ca²⁺ stores. They would cause bone loss in the mother if bone resorption were not simultaneously inhibited by an increase in the plasma calcitonin level.

The given clinical vignette is suggestive of Chvostek sign, seen in hypocalcemia due to accidental parathyroid injury during thyroid surgery. The muscle hyperexcitability seen in hypocalcemia is due to increased permeability of cells to Na⁺.

During thyroid surgery, parathyroid gland is prone to accidental injury due to proximity with the thyroid gland. Damage to the parathyroid gland will lead to a low PTH level and low Ca²⁺ level.

When the ECF concentration of Ca²⁺ falls below normal, the nervous system becomes progressively more excitable. Because there is increased membrane permeability to Na⁺. This leads to easy initiation of the action potentials.

Parathyroid adenoma is a benign tumor of the parathyroid gland, which causes primary hyperparathyroidism (not secondary).

Secondary hyperparathyroidism is characterized by high levels of parathyroid hormone, to compensate for the low levels of serum calcium, due to some other underlying condition.

Causes of secondary hyperparathyroidism include:
• Chronic kidney disease: The damaged kidneys are unable to produce sufficient amounts of the active form of vitamin D, 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol. This further causes hypocalcemia and triggers PTH secretion.
• Vitamin D deficiency: Causes hypocalcemia, which triggers the increased secretion of PTH.
• Lithium: May cause an increased set-point of calcium for parathyroid hormone suppression, which leads to parathyroid hyperplasia.

Sertoli cells express FSH receptor, whereas Leydig cells express LH receptor.

Sertoli cells are the true epithelial cells of the seminiferous epithelium and extend from basal lamina to the lumen.

Functions of Sertoli cells:
• Express FSH receptor and androgen receptor.
• Form the blood-testis barrier.
• Surround the sperm cells and provide structural support within the epithelium.
• Guide sperm cells towards the lumen as they advance to later stages of spermatogenesis.

candidates.subject: Physiology
candidates.value:
Spermiogenesis refers to the formation of spermatozoa from spermatids.

Spermiogenesis is a process by which there is a formation of extremely specialized mobile spermatozoa from spermatids. This process requires extensive remodeling or packaging of cell elements. It occurs in the recesses formed by invaginations of the Sertoli cell plasma membrane.

Maturation from spermatids to spermatozoa depends on androgen acting on Sertoli cells. When sperm maturation is complete, the cytoplasm of the Sertoli cell around sperm retracts and sperms are released into the lumen to be bathed by the luminal fluid.

The following changes occur during the formation of spermatozoa from spermatids:
• The nucleus becomes eccentric and decreases in size, and the chromatin becomes condensed.
• The cytoplasmic content is redistributed and discarded.
• The acrosome buds from the Golgi apparatus.
• The centrioles migrate to the caudal pole and form a long axial filament made of microtubules. This becomes the axoneme or major portion of the tail.

Spermiation is the release of the sperm from the Sertoli cells. During spermiation, most of the remaining cytoplasm is shed in the form of residual bodies.

Spermatogenesis refers to the formation of spermatozoa from spermatogonia.
